q: Rowlf's signed letter to Scooter says: "Per the attached order sheet, I confirm our agreement." The attached, unsigned order sheet lists 400 microphone stands at $30 each. Scooter sues Rowlf to enforce the deal. Is there a sufficient record?
o: No, because the letter and the order sheet were never stapled together.
No, because the letter itself states no price.
No, because the quantity appears only on an unsigned page.
Yes, but only if Scooter also signed the order sheet.
None of the above.
oe: Physical attachment isn't the test. The signed letter expressly refers to the sheet.
Price isn't required, and the sheet states one anyway.
The signed letter incorporates the attached sheet, so the papers are read together.
Only the party to be charged (Rowlf) must sign.
Correct. Yes: several papers can be read together if they are connected, and Rowlf's signed letter refers to the order sheet, which supplies the quantity. No choice gives that answer.

q: A contract requires delivery of a commercial espresso machine by June 30. The seller delivers on June 10, but the machine is the wrong voltage, and the buyer rejects it. On June 12, the seller notifies the buyer that it will deliver the correct model by June 25. Must the buyer accept the June 25 tender?
o: No, because cure is available only if the seller reasonably believed the first tender would be accepted.
No, because a merchant seller has no right to cure.
Yes, but only if the seller pays a penalty for the first tender.
Yes, because the time hadn't expired and the seller gave seasonable notice.
No, because the buyer's rejection ended the contract.
oe: That's the requirement for cure after the contract time (§ 2-508(2)).
Any seller may cure.
No penalty is required.
Rejection doesn't end the seller's right to cure.

q: Statler's three-year supply contract with Waldorf has a buried clause: if Waldorf fails to answer any written request for volume pricing within ten days, Statler gets a 30% discount for the rest of the term. Statler learns that Waldorf's new contracts manager doesn't know the clause exists, so Statler sends a short email asking about "pricing options" without mentioning it. The manager ignores the email, and Statler claims the discount. What is Waldorf's strongest argument?
o: Statler deliberately exploited Waldorf's known oversight during performance, which is bad faith.
Good faith requires each party to act as the other's fiduciary, so Statler had to point out the discount clause.
Statler's request was not in a signed record.
The discount clause is unconscionable.
A party may never benefit from a clause the other side has forgotten.
oe: Correct. This is Market Street: after contracting, taking advantage of a partner's oversight that you could correct at no cost is opportunistic "sharp dealing."
Market Street places good faith between a fiduciary duty and merely avoiding fraud.
Nothing in the clause or the Code requires a signature here.
Nothing suggests unfairness at the time of contracting.
Too broad. Simply benefiting from the other side's own lapse is fine (Vintage Rodeo). Deliberately inducing and exploiting it is not.

q: Before closing on a $200,000 violin warranted in the bill of sale as "an authentic Stradivarius," the seller hands Rowlf a lab report casting doubt on that claim. Rowlf closes without comment. The violin is a copy. What is the seller's best defense?
o: The warranty of authenticity was puffing.
Authenticity is an affirmation of the violin's value.
Rowlf waived the breach by closing silently.
Rowlf did not rely on the warranty at all.
None of the above.
oe: A specific written statement of authenticity is an affirmation of fact.
It's a fact about the goods, not their value.
Correct. Under Rogath, a buyer who closes knowing facts the seller disclosed that make the warranty false waives the breach unless the buyer expressly preserves its rights.
Reliance isn't the test. What matters is where Rowlf's knowledge came from.
C is correct.
topic: 5 · Express warranties — Basis of the bargain: seller's disclosure

q: Grover buys a used excavator from a dealer. A bank then sues Grover, asserting a substantial and plausible lien on the excavator. After a year of litigation, a court holds the lien invalid. Did the dealer breach the warranty of title?
o: No, because the warranty of title covers only stolen goods.
Most courts say yes, because a substantial claim breaches it even if the claim fails.
No, because the court held the lien invalid, so Grover ended up with exactly the title the dealer promised.
No, because a lien isn't a defect in title.
Yes, but only if the dealer knew of the bank's claim.
oe: It also covers liens and encumbrances the buyer didn't know of (§ 2-312(1)(b)).
Correct. § 2-312 cmt. 1: the buyer shouldn't have to litigate to protect its title.
Most courts don't require the claim to succeed.
§ 2-312(1)(b) expressly covers security interests and liens.
The seller's knowledge isn't required.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Title: colorable claim

q: Midway through a supply contract, a seller emails: "We'd like you to pay 10% more given our rising costs." A week later, it emails again: "We will make no further deliveries unless you agree to the 10% increase." Which email is a repudiation?
o: Both, because any demand for more money is a repudiation.
Neither, because the seller had a legitimate business reason to ask for more money as its costs rose.
Only the first, because it asks for more than the contract gives.
Only the second, because it conditions further performance on terms the contract doesn't require.
None of the above.
oe: Only a demand that conditions performance is.
A good reason doesn't permit conditioning performance on new terms.
Asking alone isn't repudiation.
Correct. § 2-610 cmt. 2.
D is correct.
topic: 15 · Insecurity & repudiation — Asking vs. conditioning

q: Abby hires Rosita's Remodeling to redo Abby's kitchen for $40,000. The contract allocates $31,000 to cabinets and appliances Rosita will supply and $9,000 to installation. The new oven Rosita supplied catches fire in its first week. Under amended § 2-102(2), how does Article 2 apply to Abby's warranty claim?
o: Article 2 does not apply, because a remodeling contract is a contract for services.
Real-property law governs, because the oven was installed in Abby's house.
Article 2 applies only if Rosita is a merchant who regularly deals in ovens.
Article 2 applies to the whole transaction, because the goods predominate.
Only the Article 2 provisions that relate primarily to the goods apply.
oe: The label doesn't decide it. This is a hybrid transaction, and the price allocation shows that the goods predominate.
Goods are things movable at the time of identification to the contract (§ 2-105(1)). The oven was movable then.
Scope never depends on merchant status (Problem 1-4). Merchant status matters for the merchantability warranty, not for whether Article 2 governs.
Correct. Under amended § 2-102(2), if goods predominate in a hybrid transaction, Article 2 applies to the whole deal. An agreed price allocation (here 77% to goods) usually binds (cmt. 3).
That is the rule when goods do NOT predominate. Here they do, so all of Article 2 applies.
topic: 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Hybrid: goods predominate

q: At a police auction of unclaimed property, Telly buys a laptop that turns out to have been stolen; the true owner reclaims it. The auction terms said nothing about title. Does Telly have a claim for breach of the warranty of title?
o: No, because stolen goods are not goods.
No, because the circumstances of a police auction show the seller doesn't claim title in itself.
Yes, because every seller warrants good title.
Yes, unless the auction was run by a merchant.
Yes, because no one said "as is."
oe: They are goods.
Correct. § 2-312(2): circumstances like sheriff's or police sales exclude the title warranty.
Not when circumstances show the seller doesn't claim title in itself.
Merchant status doesn't matter here.
"As is" wouldn't disclaim title anyway.
topic: 10 · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Title: police auction

q: Two merchants exchange forms. The buyer's purchase order says nothing about late payment. The seller's acknowledgment, a definite acceptance, adds: "Overdue invoices bear interest at 1.5% per month." The buyer never objects. Is the interest term part of the contract?
o: No, because an acceptance cannot add terms the offer lacked.
No, because an added term needs the offeror's express assent.
Yes, because the term is not a material alteration.
Yes, but only if the buyer signed the acknowledgment.
No, because added payment terms always materially alter a contract.
oe: That is the mirror-image rule, which § 2-207(1) rejects.
That is the rule when a non-merchant is involved. Between merchants, added terms can come in automatically.
Correct. § 2-207(2) and cmt. 5, which lists interest on overdue invoices as a term that does not materially alter the contract.
No signature is needed for an added term to become part of the contract.
Cmt. 5 says the opposite about interest on overdue invoices.
topic: 2 · Formation — Additional term: interest

q: A contract bars the buyer from assigning any rights. The seller completely fails to deliver, giving the buyer a damages claim for breach of the whole contract. The buyer assigns that claim to a collection company. Is the assignment effective?
o: Yes, despite the contract's ban.
No, because the contract bars assignment of any rights.
Yes, but only if the seller consents.
No, because damages claims are personal.
None of the above.
oe: This right is assignable despite the ban.
No consent is needed.
They are assignable.
A is correct.
topic: 13 · Assignment & delegation — Claim for breach of the whole

q: Kermit's grain sits in a public warehouse. Kermit sells it to Fozzie and, that morning, hands Fozzie a non-negotiable warehouse receipt. The warehouse hasn't been notified. That afternoon, the warehouse burns. Who most likely bears the loss?
o: The warehouse, because it's a bailee.
Fozzie, because Fozzie received a document of title.
Kermit, because title never passes while goods are in a warehouse.
Kermit, because risk doesn't pass until Fozzie has had a reasonable time to present the document.
Fozzie, because the grain was identified to the contract.
oe: The question is which party bears risk.
A non-negotiable document doesn't pass risk immediately.
Title can pass, and risk isn't tied to title anyway.
Identification doesn't pass risk.
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — Bailee: non-negotiable document

q: At a used-RV lot, the salesperson tells Animal, "The engine was completely rebuilt last spring." Animal then signs a contract stating in bold capitals: "SOLD AS IS. SELLER MAKES NO WARRANTIES, EXPRESS OR IMPLIED. THIS IS THE ENTIRE AGREEMENT." The engine was never rebuilt. What is Animal's strongest route to relief?
o: A claim that "as is" language never works against a consumer.
A fraud claim, because the parol evidence rule doesn't bar evidence of fraud.
A claim for breach of the implied warranty of merchantability.
A claim for breach of express warranty, because § 2-316(1) makes the disclaimer inoperative.
None of the above.
oe: It can work.
Correct. Problem 5-13: if the writing is final on warranties, the oral warranty is out, but fraud evidence comes in.
"As is" kills the implied warranties.
§ 2-316(1) is subject to § 2-202, which likely excludes the prior oral warranty.
B is correct.
topic: 12 · Parol evidence rule — Oral warranty vs. "as is" writing

q: A contract prices 10,000 gallons of diesel at "the State Energy Office's posted rate on the delivery date." The office stops publishing rates before delivery. The parties intended to be bound. What price applies?
o: The last rate the office published.
The price under the parties' previous contract.
Whatever price the seller names.
No price, so the contract fails.
A reasonable price at the time for delivery.
oe: That isn't the agreed standard, and the Code supplies a different fallback.
No such rule.
The seller wasn't given that power.
They intended to be bound.
Correct. § 2-305(1)(c): an agreed market or third-party standard that isn't set yields a reasonable price. Compare Problem 4-3(b).
topic: 7 · Quantity & price — Agreed index fails

q: A seller fails to deliver 1,000 widgets priced at $10 each. The buyer promptly and reasonably buys substitutes for $13 each, spending $200 to arrange the purchase, and saves $100 in freight it would have paid under the original contract. Ignoring consequential damages, what can the buyer recover under § 2-712?
oe: That leaves out the incidental expenses and the savings.
Correct. Cover minus contract price ($3,000) plus incidental damages ($200) minus expenses saved ($100).
That subtracts the $200 instead of adding it.
That forgets to subtract the $100 saved.
That's the cost of cover, not damages.
topic: 11 · Remedies & remedy limitations — Cover damages

q: Gonzo bites into a sandwich advertised as "boneless chicken breast" and is injured by a sharp bone fragment. The restaurant argues that bones are natural to chicken. Under the reasonable-expectation test, what is the most likely result?
o: Gonzo wins, because restaurants are liable for any injury caused by food.
The restaurant wins unless Gonzo proves negligence.
The restaurant wins, because a substance natural to the food, like a chicken bone, can never make food unmerchantable.
Gonzo wins, because a diner can reasonably expect a sandwich sold as boneless to have no bones.
The restaurant wins, because Gonzo should have checked the sandwich.
oe: Too broad. The food must be unmerchantable.
Merchantability doesn't require negligence.
That's the foreign-natural test.
Correct. The reasonable-expectation test (Schafer) asks what a consumer would reasonably expect, and "boneless" sets that expectation.
A diner needn't dissect a boneless sandwich.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Food: reasonable expectation

q: Gonzo sells 1,000 cases of bottled water stored at an independent warehouse. On Monday, the warehouse acknowledges to the buyer that it now holds the water for the buyer. On Wednesday, before the buyer picks it up, a roof collapse destroys the water. Who bears the loss?
o: Gonzo, because Gonzo is a merchant seller.
Gonzo, because the buyer hadn't yet paid.
The warehouse, because the water was in its possession.
Gonzo, because the buyer never received the water.
None of the above.
oe: The merchant rule applies only under § 2-509(3).
Payment doesn't affect risk.
The question is which party bears risk.
Receipt isn't the test for goods held by a bailee.
Correct. The buyer bears it: for goods held by a bailee without being moved, risk passes when the bailee acknowledges the buyer's right to possession (§ 2-509(2)(b)). No choice says that.
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — Bailee: acknowledgment

q: Scooter works full time as a stage manager but builds acoustic guitars at night and sells several every month from a booth at a regional music market. A guitar Scooter sold cracks along the neck within weeks of ordinary use. Did Scooter give an implied warranty of merchantability?
o: Yes, because every seller gives an implied warranty of merchantability.
No, because the buyer didn't tell Scooter a particular purpose.
Yes, because Scooter is a merchant in guitars.
No, because the guitars are handmade.
No, because guitar-making is not Scooter's main occupation.
oe: Only merchants for goods of that kind do.
That's a fitness requirement.
Correct. § 2-314 requires a merchant with respect to goods of that kind, and Scooter regularly makes and sells guitars.
How goods are made doesn't matter.
A day job isn't decisive (Problem 3-9's accountant-artisan).
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Merchant: regular side business

q: A seller repudiates a contract to sell 500 tons of gravel at $40 a ton. When the buyer learns of the repudiation, the market price is $46 a ton. The buyer doesn't cover. Under § 2-713, what are the buyer's basic damages, before incidental and consequential damages?
o: Nothing, because the buyer didn't cover.
None of the above.
oe: That's the contract price.
Cover is optional (§ 2-712(3)).
Correct. Market minus contract ($6) times 500 tons.
That's the market value.
C is correct.
topic: 11 · Remedies & remedy limitations — Market damages

q: Fozzie buys a used delivery van that seems fine on a test drive. Three weeks later, a hidden crack in the engine block appears and leaves the van undrivable. Fozzie promptly notifies the dealer and returns the van. Can Fozzie revoke acceptance?
o: Yes, because the hidden defect substantially impairs the van's value and Fozzie acted promptly.
No, because revocation is allowed only for defects the seller knew about.
No, because used goods can't be returned.
No, because Fozzie accepted the van after a test drive.
Yes, because any defect, hidden or not, justifies revocation if the buyer acts within 30 days of delivery.
oe: Correct. § 2-608: a nonconformity that substantially impairs value, accepted because it was hard to discover, and revoked within a reasonable time.
The seller's knowledge isn't required.
No such rule.
Revocation exists for goods already accepted.
Revocation requires substantial impairment, not just any defect.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — Revocation of acceptance

q: While negotiating to buy a used tractor from Fozzie, Gonzo realizes from Fozzie's asking price that Fozzie doesn't know the tractor's rare engine makes it worth far more. Gonzo says nothing and buys at Fozzie's price. Fozzie later claims Gonzo breached the duty of good faith. What result?
o: Gonzo wins, but only if Gonzo is a merchant.
Fozzie wins, because the tractor's true value made the price unconscionable.
Fozzie wins, because Gonzo had a duty to disclose every material fact.
Fozzie wins, because Gonzo exploited superior knowledge.
None of the above.
oe: Merchant status doesn't matter here.
A bargain price freely set by the seller isn't unconscionable.
There's no general duty to disclose in negotiation.
Exploiting superior knowledge before contracting is allowed (Market Street).

Correct. Gonzo wins: the § 1-304 duty of good faith covers performance and enforcement, not negotiation, and Market Street allows a party to use superior knowledge before contracting. No choice says that.
topic: 4 · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Good faith before contracting

q: Two merchants agree by phone that Abby's Bakery will buy 2,000 pounds of flour from Grover's Mill. Grover sends a signed confirmation stating the quantity; Abby receives and reads it the next day. Abby objects in writing 14 days later. What is the effect?
o: Abby has no statute-of-frauds defense, though Grover must still prove the oral contract.
Abby has a statute-of-frauds defense, because Abby signed nothing.
The confirmation is ineffective, because it states no price.
Abby's objection is timely, because a merchant has a reasonable time to object, and two weeks is reasonable.
Grover wins automatically, because the confirmation proves the contract.
oe: Correct. § 2-201(2): Abby didn't object within ten days. Satisfying the statute only opens the courthouse door; Grover must still prove the deal.
The merchant's-confirmation exception exists for exactly this situation.
Only quantity is essential.
The statute sets ten days.
It removes the statute-of-frauds defense, but Grover still has to prove the contract.
topic: 3 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Merchant's confirmation: late objection

q: Big Bird hires an engineering firm to design a custom irrigation system for $50,000. The price includes $6,000 for pumps and valves the firm supplies; the rest is for design work, so goods do not predominate. Under amended § 2-102(2), which of the following would NOT apply to the transaction?
o: The rules on risk of loss for the pumps and valves.
Big Bird's right to reject nonconforming pumps.
The statute of frauds (§ 2-201).
The implied warranty of merchantability for the pumps (§ 2-314).
Big Bird's remedies if the pumps are never delivered.
oe: They apply. Tender and risk of loss relate primarily to the goods (cmt. 5).
It applies. Acceptance, rejection, and cure all relate to the goods (cmt. 5).
Correct. Cmt. 5: when goods don't predominate, only the provisions relating primarily to the goods apply. The statute of frauds, the formation sections (§§ 2-204 to 2-207), and § 2-209 do not.
It applies. When goods don't predominate, the warranty provisions still apply to the goods (cmt. 5).
They apply. The buyer's remedies for nondelivery of the goods relate to the goods (cmt. 5).

q: A craft brewery supplies a regional grocery chain under an at-will arrangement with no fixed term. Encouraged by the chain's talk of a "long partnership," the brewery borrows heavily to double its capacity. Eight months later, the chain gives 90 days' notice that it is ending the arrangement, enough time to find other buyers. The brewery sues for five years of lost profits, arguing the termination was in bad faith. What is the most likely result?
o: The brewery wins, because the chain needed a good reason to terminate.
The chain wins, because termination never requires notice.
The brewery wins, because good faith bars termination before the brewery recoups its investment.
The chain wins on lost profits, because good faith doesn't override the right to end an indefinite contract on reasonable notice.
None of the above.
oe: No reason is required.
Reasonable notice is required (§ 2-309(3)).
Good faith can't override the statutory right to terminate.
Correct. This is Santa Fe Custom Shutters v. Home Depot. Claims for fraud in the inducement or inadequate notice might survive, but not five years of lost profits.
D is correct.
topic: 14 · Termination — At-will supply: heavy investment

q: Before closing on a rare first-edition comic book warranted as "unrestored," the seller tells Kermit that one grader thought the cover had been retouched. Kermit replies in writing, "I'm closing in reliance on your warranty and reserve all my rights," and closes. The cover was retouched. Can Kermit recover?
o: Yes, because the seller's disclosure was itself an express warranty.
No, because Kermit learned of the problem from the seller before closing.
Yes, because Kermit expressly reserved rights at closing.
No, because the grader's view wasn't a definite statement of fact.
No, because a buyer can't rely on a warranty it suspects is false.
oe: The disclosure warned Kermit. It didn't promise anything.
That would be waiver, except that Kermit expressly preserved the claim.
Correct. Rogath: disclosure by the seller leads to waiver unless the buyer expressly preserves its rights, as Kermit did.
The warranty ("unrestored") is the definite statement that was breached.
Rogath rejects a strict belief-in-the-truth test.
topic: 5 · Express warranties — Preserving rights at closing

q: On May 1, a seller tells Gonzo it won't deliver the July 1 shipment. On May 10, before Gonzo has canceled, bought elsewhere, or said anything else, the seller writes that it will deliver after all. Which statement is correct?
o: The seller has retracted, which reinstates the contract.
The seller may retract only with Gonzo's consent.
The retraction works only if the seller pays damages for the delay.
The repudiation became final when it was made.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. § 2-611.
No consent is needed.
No payment is required.
It can be retracted until the next performance is due.
A is correct.
topic: 15 · Insecurity & repudiation — Retraction

q: Bert trades a vintage drum kit to Ernie for Ernie's used motorcycle. No money changes hands. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Article 2 applies only to whichever item is worth more.
The exchange is a gift between friends governed by the common law, because no one paid a price.
Article 2 applies, and each party is a seller of the goods it transfers.
Article 2 doesn't apply, because no price is paid in money.
None of the above.
oe: It applies to both.
Each side gives value, so it isn't a gift.
The price can be payable in goods (§ 2-304(1)).
C is correct.
topic: 7 · Quantity & price — Price paid in goods

q: In a deal between merchants, the seller's acknowledgment adds a term letting the seller cancel the entire contract if any single invoice is paid even one day late. The buyer's order said nothing on the subject, and the buyer never objects. What is the most likely status of the term?
o: It is part of the contract unless a court finds it unconscionable.
It turns the acknowledgment into a counteroffer.
It is part of the contract, because both parties are merchants.
It is part of the contract, because the buyer did not object within a reasonable time.
It is not part of the contract, because it would materially alter the deal.
oe: The test is material alteration, not unconscionability.
An added term doesn't do that unless the acceptance is expressly conditional on assent.
Merchant status only brings added terms within § 2-207(2); a material alteration still stays out.
Silence doesn't help a term that materially alters the contract.
Correct. § 2-207(2)(b). Cmt. 4 lists a power to cancel on any late invoice as a material alteration.
topic: 2 · Formation — Material alteration

q: Gonzo orders a commercial mixer by phone, and the seller confirms the order by email, forming a contract. When the mixer arrives, the invoice in the box includes a conspicuous disclaimer of "ALL IMPLIED WARRANTIES, INCLUDING MERCHANTABILITY." Gonzo never agrees to it. Is the disclaimer part of the contract?
o: No, because merchantability can't be disclaimed between merchants.
No, because it came after formation and Gonzo never agreed to it.
Yes, because Gonzo kept the mixer.
Yes, because it is conspicuous and mentions merchantability.
None of the above.
oe: It can be.
Correct. Treated under § 2-207 or § 2-209, a later disclaimer is a material alteration or an unaccepted proposal (Problem 5-4).
Keeping the goods isn't assent to a new term.
First ask whether it's part of the contract at all.
B is correct.
topic: 10 · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Disclaimer after formation

q: On the day they sign a final but not complete contract for 1,000 jackets at $50 each, the parties also sign a separate side letter giving the buyer a $5 discount per jacket. The seller argues that the side letter contradicts the contract price. Is the side letter admissible?
o: Yes, because a contemporaneous written agreement is read together with the writing.
No, because agreements made at the same time as the writing are always excluded by the parol evidence rule.
Yes, but only if the side letter has its own merger clause.
No, because it contradicts the written price.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. The Problem 5-10 chart: a contradictory contemporaneous writing is admissible against a partial integration.
Only contemporaneous oral agreements are barred from contradicting.
No such requirement.
A contemporaneous writing is read with the main writing.
A is correct.
topic: 12 · Parol evidence rule — Contemporaneous side letter

q: Telly sends a manufacturer detailed designs and orders 5,000 toy robots built exactly to them. A toy company sues Telly for patent infringement based on the design. Telly claims the manufacturer breached the warranty against infringement. What result?
o: The manufacturer is liable only if the patent claim is proved valid.
Neither party bears any responsibility until the patent claim is resolved.
The manufacturer is liable, because every merchant warrants against infringement.
The manufacturer is liable, but Telly must share the cost of defending the suit.
None of the above.
oe: With the buyer's specs, the manufacturer isn't liable at all.
The allocation is set by § 2-312(3) now.
There's an exception when the buyer furnishes the specs.
The manufacturer isn't liable.

Correct. The manufacturer isn't liable, and Telly must hold it harmless: a buyer who furnishes specifications to the seller must protect the seller from infringement claims arising from compliance (§ 2-312(3)). No choice says that.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Infringement: buyer's specs

q: After months of negotiation, Rosita and a buyer sign a detailed deal for restaurant equipment that lets the buyer extend the closing date by giving written notice by May 1. The buyer forgets. Rosita, who did nothing to cause the lapse and said nothing about it, refuses to extend. The buyer claims Rosita acted in bad faith. What is the most likely result?
o: Rosita wins, because merely benefiting from the buyer's own missed deadline is not bad faith.
The buyer wins, because good faith lets a court excuse a missed deadline when the loss is great.
Rosita wins, because good faith doesn't apply to sophisticated parties.
The buyer wins, because Rosita's silence was sharp dealing like the tenant's in Market Street.
The buyer wins, because good faith required Rosita to remind the buyer of the deadline.
oe: Correct. Compare Vintage Rodeo: in a heavily negotiated deal, a party that simply benefits from the other side's lapse does nothing wrong. Good faith fills gaps; it doesn't rewrite express terms.
Good faith can't contradict an express term.
It applies to every contract (§ 1-304).
The tenant in Market Street deliberately induced and exploited the oversight. Rosita did nothing.
Good faith imposes no duty to be the other side's keeper.
topic: 4 · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Benefiting from a missed deadline

q: A buyer repudiates a contract in a way that substantially impairs its value to the seller. Which of the following may the seller do?
o: Resort immediately to any remedy for breach.
Urge the buyer to retract while awaiting performance.
Await the buyer's performance for a commercially reasonable time.
Suspend its own performance.
All of the above.
oe: It may, without losing its other options (§ 2-610(b)).
Correct. § 2-610 lets the aggrieved party suspend its performance and either await performance for a commercially reasonable time or resort to remedies, even after urging retraction.
topic: 15 · Insecurity & repudiation — Options after repudiation

q: A two-page form contract between a consumer and a dealer contains a boilerplate merger clause. The consumer offers evidence of an oral side term consistent with the writing. Which statement best describes the merger clause's effect?
o: It has no effect in consumer contracts.
It bars later modifications.
It bars evidence of fraud.
It conclusively makes the writing complete and exclusive.
It is strong evidence that the writing is complete and exclusive, but not conclusive.
oe: It's still evidence of integration.
That's a NOM clause.
The parol evidence rule never bars fraud evidence.
It's evidence, not a conclusive rule.
Correct. A merger clause is probative, not conclusive, especially in a short consumer form.
topic: 12 · Parol evidence rule — Merger clause: weight

q: Which of the following may the parties to a sales contract vary by agreement?
o: The default place for delivery (§ 2-308).
The rules on how a contract is formed (§§ 2-204 to 2-207).
The obligation of good faith.
The court's power to refuse to enforce an unconscionable clause (§ 2-302).
The rights of good-faith purchasers from a party with voidable title (§ 2-403).
oe: Correct. Gap fillers apply "unless otherwise agreed."
Can't be varied (Problem 5-1(b)).
It can't be disclaimed, though parties may set reasonable standards for it.
Can't be varied.
Can't be varied.

q: Fozzie, a car dealer, agrees by phone to sell a $30,000 used truck to Animal, a drummer with no business experience with vehicles. Fozzie mails Animal a signed confirmation. Animal never objects, then refuses to buy. Can Fozzie enforce the deal?
o: Yes, because Fozzie signed a record stating the quantity.
Yes, if Animal actually read the confirmation.
Yes, because Animal failed to object within ten days.
No, because Animal isn't a merchant and signed nothing.
No, because a used truck is not a good.
oe: A record must be signed by the party against whom enforcement is sought.
Reading it doesn't matter, because the exception doesn't apply to a non-merchant.
The ten-day rule binds only a merchant recipient.
Correct. § 2-201(2) requires both parties to be merchants. Fozzie's own signature binds only Fozzie.
It is a good.
topic: 3 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Confirmation to a non-merchant

q: A boat dealer's brochure describes a used 38-foot sailboat as "seaworthy and ready for offshore passages." Snuffy buys the boat after skimming the brochure but cannot show that the statement was a major reason for buying. The boat is unfit for open water. Under the view in Keith v. Buchanan, which the casebook cites, how is a court most likely to treat the brochure statement?
o: As an express warranty, but only if Snuffy proves the statement was the main reason for buying the boat.
As an express warranty that is part of the basis of the bargain without proof of specific reliance.
As neither, because a brochure isn't addressed to a particular buyer.
As an implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose.
As puffing, because "seaworthy" is general sales talk.
oe: Many courts (and cmt. 3) don't require proof of specific reliance.
Correct. The Keith view treats such a brochure statement as an affirmation of fact and doesn't require proof of reliance (cmt. 3).
Advertising and brochures can create express warranties.
It's an express statement, and nothing shows Snuffy relied on the dealer to pick a boat for a particular purpose.
It's a specific statement about the boat's condition.
topic: 5 · Express warranties — Brochure: "seaworthy"

q: Gonzo accepts a used tractor warranted to have a rebuilt engine and pays the $18,000 price. The engine was never rebuilt. As warranted, the tractor would be worth $20,000; as delivered, it's worth $13,000. What are Gonzo's basic damages under § 2-714(2)?
o: $2,000, the value as warranted minus the price.
$5,000, the price Gonzo paid minus the tractor's value as delivered.
Nothing, because Gonzo accepted the tractor.
$7,000, the value as warranted minus the value as accepted.
$18,000, the full price.
oe: That's Gonzo's bargain, not the loss.
The measure uses value as warranted, not the price.
Acceptance doesn't bar damages, given timely notice.
Gonzo kept the tractor.
topic: 11 · Remedies & remedy limitations — Accepted goods: § 2-714(2)

q: A school district contracts to buy 12,000 cartons of milk a month for the school year at a fixed price. Enrollment drops 30%, and the district orders only 8,400 cartons a month. What is the dairy's position?
o: The contract is void for mutual mistake about enrollment.
The district must take and pay for 12,000 cartons, because it agreed to a fixed quantity.
The district may cut the order but owes the dairy one month of lost profits.
The district may cut its order, because it acted in good faith.
The district may cut its order, because a 30% drop is not unreasonably disproportionate to the stated quantity.
oe: Enrollment risk is the kind of risk a fixed quantity allocates.
Correct. Problem 4-1(a): the buyer can't cut a fixed quantity without the seller's assent.
No such rule.
Good faith limits requirements contracts. This is a fixed-quantity contract.
Disproportion is a § 2-306 test, which doesn't apply to a fixed quantity.
topic: 7 · Quantity & price — Fixed quantity

q: Prairie Dawn, a consumer, orders a sofa online from Statler's Furniture. Statler's emailed confirmation accepts the order but adds: "All disputes must be brought in Statler's home county." Prairie Dawn never responds. Is the forum term part of the contract?
o: No, because Statler's confirmation was a counteroffer that ended the deal.
Yes, because the confirmation was a definite expression of acceptance that Prairie Dawn received and never disputed.
Yes, unless the term materially alters the contract.
Yes, because Prairie Dawn did not object within ten days.
No, because with a non-merchant buyer the added term is only a proposal Prairie Dawn never accepted.
oe: A definite acceptance with an added term still forms a contract (§ 2-207(1)).
That forms the contract, but it doesn't make the added term part of it.
The materiality test applies only between merchants.
The ten-day rule is from the merchant's-confirmation exception to the statute of frauds (§ 2-201(2)), not § 2-207.
Correct. § 2-207(2). The automatic inclusion rule applies only between merchants.
topic: 2 · Formation — Added term: consumer buyer

q: A law firm sells its old office copier to Prairie Dawn for $800. The copier jams constantly. Did the law firm give an implied warranty of merchantability?
o: Yes, because a law firm holds itself out as having business knowledge.
Yes, because the firm is a business that regularly buys office equipment.
Yes, because the copier is used.
No, because the firm doesn't deal in copiers.
No, because the sale was under $1,000.
oe: For merchantability, the question is whether it deals in goods of that kind.
Buying equipment for its own use doesn't make it a dealer in copiers.
Used goods carry the warranty only if the seller is a merchant.
Correct. For § 2-314, "merchant" has the narrow goods sense. An isolated sale isn't enough (though cmt. 3 says a seller must disclose known hidden defects).
No dollar threshold applies.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Isolated sale by a business

q: Telly hires a landscaper to redesign Telly's backyard. Services make up most of the $25,000 price, but the landscaper also supplies and installs a cedar swing set, which collapses in its first week and injures Telly's child. In a state that follows the gravamen-of-the-claim test, a court would most likely:
o: Apply the Article 2 merchantability warranty, because the claim concerns the swing set.
Apply Article 2 only if the swing set made up more than half of the contract price.
Apply Article 2 to the whole contract, including claims about the landscape design.
Refuse to apply Article 2, because services predominate in the contract taken as a whole, so no part of it is a sale.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Under the gravamen test (Anthony Pools), the court asks whether the claim relates to the goods or the services. A defective swing set is a goods claim, so the Article 2 warranty applies even though services predominate.
That mixes in the predominance factors. The gravamen test asks what the claim is about.
The gravamen test applies Article 2 only to claims about the goods. A claim about the design would be a services claim.
That is the predominant-purpose test, which is all-or-nothing. The gravamen test looks at the claim, not the whole contract.
A is correct.
topic: 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Gravamen of the claim

q: Under a contract of indefinite duration, a bakery delivers bread to Ernie's diner every day. One morning, the bakery tells Ernie it will stop delivering that afternoon, leaving Ernie no time to find another supplier. The contract says nothing about termination. Which statement is correct?
o: The bakery may stop at any time without liability.
The bakery may not terminate until the contract has run a reasonable time.
The bakery must keep supplying bread for at least a year.
The bakery may terminate but owes Ernie reasonable notice.
None of the above.
oe: It may terminate at any time, but only with reasonable notice.
Santa Fe: the contract needn't have run a reasonable time.
No minimum term exists.
D is correct.
topic: 14 · Termination — Termination without notice

q: A restaurant rightfully rejects 30 cases of imported wine and notifies the seller. Which of the following may the restaurant NOT do with the rejected wine?
o: Hold it with reasonable care for the seller to remove.
Follow the seller's reasonable instructions for returning it.
Serve some of it to customers while waiting for the seller.
Resell it for the seller's account if the seller gives no instructions within a reasonable time.
Store it for the seller's account if the seller gives no instructions.
oe: A merchant buyer must (§ 2-603(1)).
Correct. After rejection, any exercise of ownership by the buyer is wrongful against the seller (§ 2-602(2)(a)).
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — Duties after rejection

q: Herry accepts a $50,000 boat, discovers a hidden hull defect that substantially impairs its value, and rightfully revokes acceptance. Before the seller retrieves the boat, a fire at Herry's dock destroys it. Herry's insurance covers $30,000. Who bears the remaining $20,000?
o: Herry, because the boat was in Herry's possession.
The insurance company must pay the full $50,000.
The seller, to the extent Herry's insurance falls short.
Herry, because the revocation wasn't complete until the seller took the boat back.
Herry and the seller split the $20,000.
oe: After rightful revocation, § 2-510(2) treats risk as on the seller to the extent of the insurance gap.
Insurance covers only what the policy covers.
The revocation was effective once Herry notified the seller.
No splitting rule.
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — Revocation and insurance

q: Bunsen signs a contract to buy a used forklift from a dealer. The contract says nothing about delivery, the parties have never dealt before, and no trade usage applies. The dealer tells Bunsen to come get it; Bunsen insists the dealer deliver it. If neither budges, who is in breach?
o: Neither, because a court will split the cost of delivery.
Bunsen, because unless otherwise agreed, the place for delivery is the seller's place of business.
The dealer, because sellers must bring the goods to the buyer.
Neither, because the contract fails without a delivery term.
The dealer, because unless the parties agree otherwise, the default place for delivery is the buyer's place of business.
oe: No such rule.
Correct. § 2-308(a). Problem 3-8(A): with no course of dealing or usage to fill the gap, the buyer who refuses to pick up is in breach.
Not by default.
Open terms don't defeat a contract; gap fillers apply.
It's the seller's place.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Place of delivery gap filler

q: A hardware-store clerk tells Ernie several things about a portable generator. Which is MOST likely an express warranty?
o: "It's a great value at this price."
"It runs 12 hours on one tank at half load."
"You'll love having this when the power goes out."
"I'd buy this one myself."
"This is the best generator on the market."
oe: An affirmation of value, which § 2-313(2) excludes.
Correct. It's specific and measurable, an affirmation of fact relating to the goods (§ 2-313(1)(a)).
Opinion and sales talk.
The clerk's opinion or commendation.
A general superlative: puffing.
topic: 5 · Express warranties — Fact vs. puffing

q: A seafood company tells a trailer dealer it needs refrigerated trailers to haul live lobsters in seawater tanks over long distances. The dealer recommends a model, which the company buys in reliance. The trailers keep lobsters cold but can't keep them alive. The dealer argues that hauling seafood is the ordinary use of refrigerated trailers, so only merchantability could apply. What is the best response?
o: A fitness warranty arises only if the buyer's use is unique to that buyer.
The dealer is right, because hauling seafood is the ordinary use of refrigerated trailers, so no fitness warranty can arise.
The purpose need not be unique; it need only differ from the goods' customary use, a question of fact.
A fitness warranty arises whenever the seller is a merchant.
None of the above.
oe: Uniqueness isn't required.
Ingram River rejected that argument as a matter of law.

Correct. This is Ingram River: whether the use is "particular" depends on how the goods are characterized (tank barges vs. heating-coil barges), and the use need only be sufficiently different from customary use.
Fitness turns on purpose and reliance, not merchant status.
C is correct.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Particular vs. ordinary purpose

q: Which of the following is NOT part of the duty of good faith that the UCC imposes on every contract?
o: A duty to put the other party's interests ahead of one's own.
Observance of reasonable commercial standards of fair dealing.
A duty that applies when enforcing the contract.
A duty that applies when performing the contract.
Honesty in fact in the conduct concerned.
oe: Correct. That's a fiduciary duty, which good faith is not.
Part of it: the objective prong.
Part of it. § 1-304 covers performance and enforcement.
Part of it.
Part of it: the subjective prong (§ 1-201(b)(20)).
topic: 4 · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Good faith: elements

q: A contract for a complex industrial press requires the buyer to report any defect "within 24 hours after delivery or the claim is waived." The press can't be fully tested until at least two weeks after installation. Is the 24-hour term likely enforceable?
o: Yes, because parties may always fix the time for any act.
Yes, because the buyer could hire testers to work around the clock.
Yes, because both parties are merchants.
No, because notice periods can't be shortened by agreement.
None of the above.
oe: Only if the time isn't manifestly unreasonable.
Testing the press takes two weeks regardless.
Merchant status doesn't save a manifestly unreasonable time.
They can, within reason.

Correct. Likely not: parties may fix a time for a "reasonable time" only if it isn't manifestly unreasonable (§ 1-302(b)), and 24 hours is unreasonable for a press that takes two weeks to test. No choice says that.
topic: 10 · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Fixing a "reasonable time"

q: A contract's only clause on the subject says: "This contract may not be amended except by a writing signed by both parties." The buyer offers evidence of a consistent oral term agreed before signing. Does the clause bar that evidence?
o: Yes, because it is a merger clause.
Yes, because it requires every term to be in writing.
Yes, because the clause shows the writing was meant to be complete.
No, because the clause is unenforceable.
None of the above.
oe: It's a NOM clause.
It addresses amendments only.
It speaks to future changes, not to completeness.
NOM clauses are enforceable (§ 2-209(2)).
Correct. It doesn't bar the evidence: a no-oral-modification clause governs later changes, not prior agreements (Problem 5-11, clause 4). No choice says that.
topic: 12 · Parol evidence rule — NOM clause is not a merger clause

q: Rosita contracts to buy 100 custom racks from a manufacturer, which finishes them and tags them for Rosita. Rosita then repudiates. Two weeks later, while the manufacturer arranges a resale, a fire destroys the racks. The manufacturer's insurance covers only half their value. Who bears the uninsured half?
o: The manufacturer, because the racks never left its plant.
Rosita, for the full value, because the breaching party bears all losses.
The manufacturer, because it is a merchant seller.
Rosita, because a repudiating buyer bears the risk of conforming, identified goods for a commercially reasonable time, to the extent the seller's insurance falls short.
None of the above.
oe: The breaching buyer bears some risk under § 2-510(3).
Only to the extent of the seller's insurance deficiency.
The merchant rule doesn't apply when the buyer is in breach.
D is correct.
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — Buyer repudiates; identified goods

q: Midway through a two-year supply contract, Big Bird's supplier ships three defective loads, and Big Bird ends the contract because of them. How is Big Bird's action best classified, and what happens to Big Bird's damages claim for the defective loads?
o: Cancellation; Big Bird must choose between ending the contract and suing for damages.
Rescission; the parties are put back where they started.
Cancellation; Big Bird keeps its remedies for the breach.
Termination; Big Bird keeps only a right to a refund.
Termination; Big Bird loses its damages claim.
oe: Big Bird may do both.
The Code's terms here are cancellation and termination.
Correct. § 2-106(4): cancellation is ending the contract for breach, and the canceling party keeps its remedies.
It's cancellation, with full remedies.
Ending a contract for breach is cancellation.
topic: 14 · Termination — Cancellation vs. termination

q: Elmo agrees to sell Grover 200 bushels of apples, to be picked up at Elmo's orchard. At 9 a.m. Elmo calls: "They're ready, but if you're not here by 10, I'll sell them to someone else." Grover is three hours away. Has Elmo made a proper tender?
o: Yes, because the apples conformed and Grover was notified.
No, because Elmo had to deliver the apples to Grover.
No, because Elmo must hold the apples long enough for Grover to get there.
Yes, because the place of delivery is the seller's place of business, and Grover was told the apples were ready.
None of the above.
oe: Tender also requires holding the goods available long enough.
The contract made the orchard the place for delivery.
Correct. § 2-503(1)(a). Compare Problem 4-4's "pick it up within 2 hours."
That sets the place, not how long the goods must be held.
C is correct.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — Tender: holding period

q: Kermit repudiates a contract to buy 200 guitars at $500 each. After notifying Kermit, the seller resells them in a commercially reasonable private sale for $430 each, spending $1,000 on the resale. What may the seller recover?
oe: That leaves out the incidental expenses.
Correct. § 2-706: contract minus resale ($70 × 200 = $14,000) plus incidental damages ($1,000).
That's the resale proceeds.
That subtracts the expenses instead of adding them.
That's the contract price.
topic: 11 · Remedies & remedy limitations — Seller's resale

q: Statler's purchase order (the offer) says: "Seller's acceptance is limited to the terms of this order." Waldorf's acknowledgment accepts but adds a modest, customary force-majeure clause. Both are merchants, and Statler never objects. Is the force-majeure clause part of the contract?
o: No, because force-majeure clauses are not allowed in sales contracts.
No, because the offer expressly limited acceptance to its own terms.
Yes, because a reasonable force-majeure clause is not a material alteration.
Yes, because Statler never objected to it.
None of the above.
oe: They are allowed, and § 2-615 even assumes such allocations.
Correct. § 2-207(2)(a). An offer that expressly limits acceptance to its terms keeps added terms out, however reasonable.
True of the clause (cmt. 5), but the offer itself shut out added terms.
An objection isn't needed when the offer already limits acceptance to its terms.
B is correct.
topic: 2 · Formation — Offer limits acceptance

q: Gonzo owns a farm with a gravel pit. Gonzo agrees to sell Animal 5,000 tons of gravel, which Animal will dig out and haul away with Animal's own equipment. Is this a sale of goods under Article 2?
o: Yes, because gravel is movable once it is dug out.
Yes, because things attached to realty are always goods under § 2-107, whoever removes them from the land.
Yes, but only if Gonzo regularly sells gravel.
No, because minerals are goods only if the seller severs them, and Animal will do the digging.
No, because gravel is not a "thing" under § 2-105.
oe: Minerals are a special case. Under § 2-107(1), they are goods only if the seller severs them.
Only some are. Timber and crops are goods whoever severs them (§ 2-107(2)); minerals and structures are goods only if the seller severs them (§ 2-107(1)).
Article 2's scope never depends on merchant status.
Correct. § 2-107(1). Because the buyer extracts the gravel, the deal is a sale of an interest in land.
Gravel is a thing. The issue is who severs it from the land.
topic: 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Minerals: buyer severs

q: Bunsen rejects a shipment of beakers with a one-line email: "Rejected: nonconforming." The only problem was a missing set of lids, which the seller could easily have shipped. In litigation, Bunsen relies on the missing lids to justify the rejection. What result?
o: Bunsen's rejection was ineffective because it was sent by email.
Bunsen may rely on the defect, but only to reduce the price.
Bunsen may rely on the defect, because a rejection notice need not give reasons.
Bunsen may rely on the defect, because any nonconformity justifies rejection.
None of the above.
oe: Email is fine.
No such middle ground.
It must state defects that the seller could have cured if told.
Not if Bunsen failed to state a curable defect.

Correct. Bunsen can't rely on the missing lids: a buyer who fails to state a particular defect that the seller could have cured if seasonably told may not use it to justify rejection (§ 2-605(1)(a)). No choice says that.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — Failure to particularize

q: Under a contract for four quarterly installments of pumps, the seller emails that the first installment will be three weeks late but that it will catch up by the second. The buyer, who has since realized it needs only half the pumps, wants to cancel the whole contract. What is the buyer's best course?
o: Cancel the whole contract, because the buyer's reduced needs are a valid reason.
Demand assurance in writing and reserve its rights.
Do nothing and accept late delivery, because the seller promised to catch up.
Cancel the whole contract now, because any repudiation lets the buyer cancel.
None of the above.
oe: They aren't a legal ground for cancellation.
Correct. Problem 6-5: don't cancel yet; demand assurance under § 2-609 and reserve rights (§§ 2-610, 2-612).
The buyer can protect itself without giving up rights.
Canceling the whole requires substantial impairment of the whole contract.
B is correct.
topic: 15 · Insecurity & repudiation — One late installment

q: In the trade of breeding show dogs, sellers customarily provide registration papers with every purebred puppy. Fozzie buys a puppy from a breeder; the contract says nothing about papers, and the breeder refuses to provide them. What is Fozzie's best claim?
o: Breach of an implied warranty arising from usage of trade.
Breach of an express warranty by description.
No claim, because the contract says nothing about papers.
Breach of the warranty of title.
Breach of the warranty of fitness, because show dogs have a particular purpose.
oe: Correct. § 2-314(3): other implied warranties may arise from course of dealing or usage of trade (cmt. 12 uses pedigree papers as the example).
"Purebred" describes the dog's breeding, not paperwork.
Usage of trade fills the silence.
Fozzie owns the puppy. Registration papers aren't title.
Nothing shows reliance on the breeder's judgment for a particular purpose.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Implied warranty from usage

q: A youth league orders 300 jerseys printed with its name, logo, and players' numbers for $6,000 by phone. After the printer has printed 120 jerseys, the league calls to cancel. The league signed nothing. Can the printer enforce the contract?
o: No, because the printer must finish all 300 before the exception applies.
No, because the league never signed a record.
Yes, but only for the 120 jerseys already printed.
Yes, because the jerseys are made for the league, unsuitable for others, and substantially begun before the cancellation.
Yes, because the printer is a merchant.
oe: A substantial beginning is enough.
An exception applies.
§ 2-201(3)(a) makes the contract enforceable, not just the part already made.
Correct. § 2-201(3)(a): specially made goods, not suitable for sale to others in the ordinary course, and a substantial beginning before notice of repudiation.
Merchant status alone doesn't satisfy the statute.
topic: 3 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Specially manufactured goods

q: Bunsen orders 200 steel brackets from a fabricator and supplies detailed engineering drawings specifying the steel grade and thickness. The brackets match the drawings exactly but bend under the load Bunsen intended. Did the fabricator breach a warranty of fitness for a particular purpose?
o: No, because a fabricator isn't a merchant.
No, because Bunsen relied on its own specs.
Yes, because the brackets failed in use.
Yes, because merchantability and fitness always arise together.
Yes, because the fabricator knew how Bunsen would use the brackets.
oe: Fitness doesn't require a merchant, and a fabricator likely is one anyway.
Correct. A buyer who furnishes precise specs doesn't rely on the seller (§ 2-315).
Failure alone doesn't prove a fitness warranty arose.
They have different requirements.
Knowing the purpose isn't enough without reliance on the seller's judgment.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Fitness: buyer's own specs

q: Statler sells Waldorf a specific antique carriage that both know, when they contract, is stored in a barn in another county. The contract says nothing about delivery. Where is the place for delivery?
o: Statler's place of business.
Wherever Waldorf reasonably designates.
The barn where the carriage is stored.
Waldorf's residence.
The nearest carrier's terminal.
oe: That's the default only if the goods aren't known to be elsewhere.
No such rule.
Correct. § 2-308(b): for identified goods both parties know are elsewhere at contracting, that place is the place for delivery.
Never the default.
No shipment is required here.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — Identified goods stored elsewhere

q: A piano store with an unlimited supply of a popular model contracts to sell one to Rowlf for $8,000. Rowlf repudiates, and the store sells that piano the next day to another customer at the same price. The store's profit on each sale is $2,000. What is the store's best measure of damages?
o: $8,000, the price under § 2-709.
Nothing, because it resold at the same price.
$4,000, double the lost profit, as a penalty for repudiation.
The contract price minus the market price.
None of the above.
oe: Price is available only in limited cases, like accepted goods.
The resale would have happened anyway, so it didn't replace Rowlf's sale.
Damages aren't punitive.
That's zero here and doesn't reflect the lost sale.
Correct. The store recovers its $2,000 lost profit under § 2-708(2): a lost-volume seller would have made both sales, so the resale doesn't make it whole. No choice says that.
topic: 11 · Remedies & remedy limitations — Lost-volume seller

q: Telly sues Zoe to enforce an oral contract for 500 bags of potting soil. In a deposition, Zoe testifies: "We agreed on 300 bags, not 500." Zoe signed nothing. How much, if anything, can Telly enforce?
o: Nothing, because Zoe disputes the quantity.
300 bags, the quantity Zoe admitted.
500 bags, because an admission removes the statute of frauds entirely.
Nothing, because admissions count only if made in a pleading.
None of the above.
oe: Zoe admitted a contract for 300 bags.
Correct. § 2-201(3)(b). Testimony in a deposition counts as an admission in court.
The admission exception is limited to the quantity admitted.
An admission "in pleading, testimony or otherwise in court" counts.
B is correct.
topic: 3 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Admission

q: A supply agreement of indefinite duration lets the large buyer terminate "at any time, without any notice." The small supplier, which depends on the buyer for 90% of its sales, had no power to negotiate. The buyer terminates without notice. Is the no-notice term enforceable?
o: No, if waiving notice would be unconscionable here.
Yes, because the contract was of indefinite duration.
No, because termination always requires 30 days' notice.
Yes, because parties may always waive notice.
None of the above.
oe: That's when the notice rule applies.
The standard is reasonable notice, not 30 days.
Not if waiving notice would be unconscionable.
A is correct.
topic: 14 · Termination — Waiving notice of termination

q: Oscar buys a jacket whose hang tag reads "100% merino wool." The jacket is half acrylic. The clerk said nothing about the fabric, and Oscar never asked. Has the store made an express warranty?
o: No, because the clerk made no oral statement.
Yes, by description of the goods.
Yes, but only if the store intended the tag as a warranty.
No, because Oscar never asked about the fabric.
No, because a label creates only an implied warranty.
oe: Words on a tag count. No oral statement is needed.
Intent to warrant isn't required (§ 2-313(2)).
Statements need not respond to a question.
A label can support an implied-warranty claim too (§ 2-314(2)(f)), but the description itself is an express warranty.
topic: 5 · Express warranties — Description: label

q: A complete and exclusive contract for monthly deliveries of printer toner says nothing about delivery time. For eight months, the seller always delivered before 9 a.m., and the buyer accepted without comment. In month nine, the seller delivers at 4 p.m. Can the buyer use the earlier pattern to show what the agreement requires?
o: Yes, but only if the pattern lasted at least a year.
Yes, because course of performance can supplement it.
No, because the writing is complete and exclusive.
No, because course of performance requires prior contracts.
None of the above.
oe: Repeated occasions with acquiescence suffice; there's no time minimum.
Course of performance can still come in.
That's course of dealing.
B is correct.
topic: 12 · Parol evidence rule — Course of performance supplements

q: Beaker, a lab-supply merchant, signs a quote form supplied by the buyer, Bunsen. A printed line on Bunsen's form, above Beaker's only signature, says the quote "will be held open for 60 days." Two weeks later, before Bunsen accepts, Beaker revokes. Was the revocation effective?
o: No, because Bunsen relied on the quote.
No, because a merchant's signed firm offer is irrevocable for the stated time, without any need for consideration.
Yes, because Bunsen gave no consideration to keep the offer open, so it was an ordinary revocable offer.
Yes, because the assurance was on a form the offeree supplied and Beaker did not separately sign it.
No, because 60 days is within the three-month limit.
oe: Nothing shows reliance, and a firm offer doesn't depend on it anyway.
That is the general rule, but it has an exception for assurances on the offeree's form.
A merchant's firm offer needs no consideration. The problem is the missing separate signature.
Correct. § 2-205: an assurance on a form supplied by the offeree must be separately signed by the offeror.
The cap matters only if the firm offer is otherwise valid.
topic: 2 · Formation — Firm offer on offeree's form

q: At an estate liquidation, Waldorf buys an antique clock under a signed bill of sale stating: "Seller transfers only whatever right, title, and interest the estate may have, and makes no warranty of title." The price is well below market because the ownership records are missing. A third party proves it owns the clock. Does Waldorf have a claim for breach of the warranty of title?
o: No, because the bill of sale specifically disclaims the warranty of title.
No, because estate and liquidation sales never carry any warranties, whatever the bill of sale says.
Yes, because the bill of sale didn't say "as is."
Yes, because the warranty of title can't be disclaimed.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. § 2-312(2). Problem 5-5: a buyer may accept such a disclaimer when provenance is uncertain and the price reflects the risk.
Circumstances alone may suffice in some sales, but here the specific language does the work.
"As is" isn't how to disclaim title.
It can, by specific language or circumstances.
A is correct.
topic: 10 · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Title disclaimer by specific language

q: Abby and a supplier sign a contract for 600 lamps to be delivered June 1. It says: "No modification is effective unless in a signed record." By phone, they agree to move delivery to June 20. On June 2, Abby sues for late delivery, arguing that the phone agreement was ineffective. What is the supplier's best argument?
o: Even if the oral change fails under the NOM clause, it can operate as a waiver of the June 1 date.
The NOM clause is unenforceable between merchants.
The phone agreement was a valid modification, because modifications need no consideration under § 2-209(1).
The parol evidence rule bars proof of the June 1 date.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. § 2-209(4): an attempted modification that fails under the NOM clause can still be a waiver.
NOM clauses are enforceable under § 2-209(2).
The NOM clause bars an unwritten modification (§ 2-209(2)).
The June 1 date is in the writing. The parol evidence rule doesn't touch later agreements anyway.
A is correct.
topic: 4 · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — NOM clause; failed modification as waiver

q: A buyer with reasonable grounds for insecurity demands assurance from a seller with a 20-year record of reliable performance. The seller responds with a detailed written production schedule and a firm commitment to deliver on time. Is this adequate assurance?
o: No, because adequate assurance requires a letter of credit.
Yes, because any written response is adequate.
Likely yes, given the seller's long record of reliable performance.
No, because a mere promise to perform, however detailed, is never adequate assurance under § 2-609.
None of the above.
oe: No particular form is required.
Adequacy depends on the circumstances.
Correct. § 2-609 cmt. 4.
It can be, depending on the party and the facts.
C is correct.
topic: 15 · Insecurity & repudiation — Adequacy and reputation

q: Miss Piggy's Bakery has a two-year contract to buy "all the flour it requires" from a mill at a fixed $20 a bag, with an estimate of 1,000 bags a month based on its baking. Flour prices jump to $45. Miss Piggy then orders 2,500 bags a month, planning to resell the extra to other bakeries. Must the mill fill the orders?
o: No, because buying extra to resell at market is not a good-faith requirement and is disproportionate to the estimate.
No, because requirements contracts become unenforceable when the market moves.
Yes, because a requirements buyer may order whatever it needs.
Yes, because the contract states only an estimate, not a cap.
Yes, but only at the market price for the extra bags.
oe: Correct. This is Orange & Rockland: a buyer can't use a fixed-price requirements contract to speculate when the market rises.
The contract is enforceable. The excess is what's limited.
Only requirements that occur in good faith, and not unreasonably disproportionate to the estimate.
The estimate is the yardstick for disproportion (§ 2-306(1)).
§ 2-306 doesn't reprice the excess; it limits the quantity.
topic: 7 · Quantity & price — Requirements: buying to resell

q: Rowlf contracts to sell Scooter the pumpkin crop now growing on Rowlf's farm. Scooter will harvest the pumpkins in October. Which law governs the sale?
o: Article 2 governs, but only if the crop is sold before it is planted.
Article 2 governs only if Rowlf harvests the pumpkins before delivery.
Real-property law governs until the pumpkins are harvested.
Real-property law governs, because Scooter, not Rowlf, will sever the crop.
None of the above.
oe: Timing of the sale doesn't matter. Growing crops are goods.
That is the rule for minerals and structures (§ 2-107(1)), not crops.
Growing crops are goods even while attached (§ 2-105(1)).
Who severs matters only for minerals and structures. Crops are goods whoever severs them (§ 2-107(2)).
Correct. Article 2 governs. Growing crops are goods (§ 2-105(1)), and under § 2-107(2) they are goods whether the buyer or the seller severs them. No choice says that.
topic: 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Crops: either party severs

q: A gallery lets the Count take home a sculpture "on approval" for two weeks to see whether it suits the Count's living room. On day five, before the Count decides, a burglar steals it. Who bears the loss?
o: The Count, because the Count had possession.
The Count, because the gallery delivered the sculpture.
The gallery, until the Count accepts.
The Count, because using the sculpture as decor was an acceptance.
None of the above.
oe: On approval, risk stays with the seller until acceptance.
Delivery doesn't pass risk on a sale on approval.
Use consistent with the trial isn't acceptance (§ 2-327(1)(b)).
C is correct.
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — Sale on approval

q: Snuffy's Fencing receives a shipment of fence posts that fully conform to the contract. Having found a cheaper supplier, Snuffy's Fencing promptly notifies the seller that it rejects them. What is the effect?
o: The rejection is rightful, because a buyer may reject for any reason before acceptance.
It's effective but wrongful, so Snuffy's Fencing is in breach.
The rejection is rightful unless the seller can show bad faith.
The rejection is ineffective, so Snuffy's Fencing has accepted the posts.
None of the above.
oe: Only nonconforming goods may be rightfully rejected.
Correct. Rejecting conforming goods can be effective but wrongful, which is a buyer's breach (§ 2-703).
The posts conform, so the rejection is wrongful regardless.
A timely, properly notified rejection is effective even if wrongful.
B is correct.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — Wrongful but effective rejection

q: A contract says: "Seller's sole liability for defective goods is to repair or replace them." The buyer argues that the clause is ineffective because it is not conspicuous and doesn't mention merchantability. What is the best response?
o: The clause is a remedy limitation under § 2-719, not a disclaimer, so it needn't be conspicuous or mention merchantability.
The clause is void, because parties can't limit remedies for breach of warranty.
The buyer is right, because every limit on warranty liability must satisfy § 2-316.
The clause disclaims all implied warranties.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. A disclaimer removes the breach; a limitation caps damages after a breach. Remedy limits needn't be conspicuous.
§ 2-719 allows it.
§ 2-316 governs disclaimers, not remedy limits.
It limits the remedy; it doesn't disclaim warranties.
A is correct.
topic: 10 · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Disclaimer vs. remedy limitation

q: Miss Piggy's contract to buy a custom gown says: "Risk of loss passes to Buyer when this contract is signed." The seller is a merchant. The gown is finished, but before Miss Piggy picks it up, it is destroyed in a fire at the seller's shop. Who bears the loss?
o: Miss Piggy, but only if the gown had been paid for.
Miss Piggy, because the parties' agreement on risk of loss controls over the default rules.
The seller, because the risk-of-loss rules are mandatory and can't be shifted by a clause in the contract.
The seller, because a merchant seller keeps the risk until the buyer receives the goods.
None of the above.
oe: Payment doesn't matter.
They can.
That's the default, and the parties agreed otherwise.
B is correct.
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — Agreement on risk

q: A seller delivers defective packaging machinery, and the buyer rightfully rejects it. Which of the buyer's losses is CONSEQUENTIAL rather than incidental?
o: Commissions paid to a broker to arrange substitute packaging machinery.
The cost of shipping the machinery back.
Profits lost while the buyer's production line sat idle.
Storage fees for the rejected machinery.
Expenses of inspecting the machinery.
oe: Incidental: costs of effecting cover.
Incidental.
Correct. Lost profits from a shutdown are consequential (§ 2-715(2)).
Incidental (§ 2-715(1)).
Incidental.
topic: 11 · Remedies & remedy limitations — Incidental vs. consequential

q: A contract to supply flowers to a hotel "ends automatically if the hotel closes its banquet hall." The hotel closes the hall and stops ordering without telling the florist in advance. Does the florist have a claim for lack of notice?
o: Yes, because the hotel acted in bad faith.
No, because the florist could have asked whether the hall was closing.
Yes, because termination always requires reasonable notice.
Yes, because the hotel had to give 30 days' notice.
None of the above.
oe: Nothing suggests bad faith.
That isn't the reason.
Not termination on an agreed event.
No 30-day rule.
Correct. No claim: the reasonable-notice requirement of § 2-309(3) doesn't apply when a contract ends on the happening of an agreed event. No choice says that.
topic: 14 · Termination — Termination on an agreed event

q: Ernie orally agrees to buy 100 folding chairs from Bert for $2,500. Bert delivers 40 chairs, and Ernie accepts them. Ernie then refuses the rest, and Bert sues for all 100. Ernie signed nothing. What can Bert enforce?
o: The full contract, because accepting some chairs confirms the deal.
The full contract, if Bert proves the oral deal by clear evidence.
The contract as to the 40 chairs Ernie received and accepted.
Nothing, because Ernie never paid.
Nothing, because part performance applies only to specially manufactured goods.
oe: Part performance reaches only the goods accepted.
Stronger proof doesn't get around the statute.
Correct. § 2-201(3)(c): enforceable only for goods paid for and accepted or received and accepted.
Received and accepted is enough.
Those are separate exceptions.
topic: 3 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Received and accepted

q: A contract calls for 500 folding tables and says nothing about delivery in lots. The seller arrives with 250 tables and promises the rest next week. The buyer refuses to take any. Is the buyer in breach?
o: No, because the seller had to deliver to the buyer's place of business.
Yes, unless the buyer pays for the 250 tables.
Yes, because the shortfall is minor and curable.
No, because all must come in one delivery.
Yes, because a buyer must accept partial deliveries.
oe: Place isn't the issue.
The buyer need not take or pay for a partial tender.
The buyer may still insist on a single delivery.
Correct. § 2-307.
Not unless the contract provides for them.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — Single delivery

q: Abby buys a sofa from Statler's Furniture and pays in full. Statler's says the sofa is ready and Abby can pick it up anytime. Before Abby arrives, a burst pipe floods the store and ruins the sofa. Who bears the loss?
o: Abby, because Statler's tendered the sofa by telling Abby it was ready for pickup before the flood.
Abby and Statler's split it equally.
Statler's, because a merchant seller keeps the risk until the buyer receives the goods.
Statler's, because title hadn't passed to Abby.
Abby, because Abby had paid in full.
oe: Tender passes risk only from a non-merchant seller.
No splitting rule.
Correct. § 2-509(3). The merchant still controls and can insure the goods (cmt. 3).
Risk of loss isn't tied to title.
Payment doesn't shift risk.
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — Merchant seller: buyer paid

q: The Count, an antiques dealer, contracts to sell Telly a specific grandfather clock, to be picked up the next week. Before pickup, lightning strikes the shop and destroys the clock. Neither party was at fault. What is the effect?
o: The Count is in breach, because a merchant seller bears the risk until receipt.
The contract is avoided, because identified goods were totally destroyed without fault before risk passed.
Telly must pay, because the clock was identified to the contract.
The Count must deliver a comparable clock.
None of the above.
oe: Risk was the Count's, but § 2-613 excuses the Count.
Correct. § 2-613(a); Problem 6-6(a).
Risk hadn't passed to Telly.
The contract was for this unique clock.
B is correct.
topic: 16 · Excuse from performance — Casualty: no fault

q: Which of the following is a sale of "goods" under § 2-105?
o: A lab buys liquid nitrogen in pressurized tanks from a gas supplier.
Prairie Dawn buys a landlord's right to collect next year's rent from a tenant.
Zoe buys a promissory note payable to the seller.
Herry buys certificated shares in a closely held corporation.
All of the above.
oe: Correct. Liquids and gases are movable things, so they are goods (Problem 1-1's oxygen and isotopes).
A right to payment is a thing in action, not a movable thing.
A note is a thing in action (and an Article 3 instrument), which § 2-105(1) excludes.
Investment securities are excluded; Article 8 governs them.
Only A is a sale of goods.
topic: 1 · The UCC & which law governs — What is a "good"

q: On March 1, Rosita, who sells restaurant equipment, emails Herry a signed offer to sell a walk-in freezer for $9,000, adding, "I'll hold this price open for you." No time is stated. On March 10, Rosita emails that the offer is revoked. On March 12, Herry accepts. Is there a contract?
o: Yes, because the offer was irrevocable for a reasonable time, which ten days likely did not exceed.
No, because Herry gave no consideration to hold the offer open.
Yes, because a firm offer that states no time stays open for exactly three months, and only ten days had passed.
No, because an email is not a signed record.
No, because an offer that states no time may be revoked at any time.
oe: Correct. § 2-205: with no stated time, a merchant's signed firm offer is irrevocable for a reasonable time, never more than three months.
A firm offer needs no consideration.
Three months is the cap, not the default. The period is a reasonable time.
An email is a record, and a typed name can be a signature.
Not a merchant's firm offer. It stays open for a reasonable time.
topic: 2 · Formation — Firm offer: no time stated

q: Abby picks floor tile for a café from a sample board at a tile store. The delivered tile is noticeably thinner and a different shade than the sample. No one said anything about thickness or color. What is Abby's best claim?
o: Breach of the implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose, since Abby needed tile for a café.
Breach of the warranty of title.
Breach of an express warranty that the whole of the goods will conform to the sample.
No claim, because no one made an affirmation of fact.
None of the above.
oe: Nothing shows a particular purpose or reliance on the seller's judgment.
Title isn't in question.
Correct. § 2-313(1)(c): a sample that is part of the basis of the bargain creates an express warranty.
A sample creates a warranty without any words.
C is correct.
topic: 5 · Express warranties — Sample

q: Oscar's contract to sell 300 trash cans to a city says: "Any assignment by Seller of its rights is prohibited and void." Oscar assigns its right to payment to a finance company, which notifies the city. Which statement is correct?
o: The city may pay either Oscar or the finance company.
The assignment is void, as the contract says.
The assignment is effective, but Oscar is liable to the city for breach.
The assignment is effective, and the city must pay the finance company.
None of the above.
oe: After notice, it must pay the assignee.
A term barring assignment of a right to payment is ineffective.
§ 9-406(d) makes the ban ineffective, so the assignment isn't a breach either.
Correct. § 9-406(d); Problem 6-2(b).
D is correct.
topic: 13 · Assignment & delegation — Ban on assigning payment rights

q: Kermit tells a neighbor that Kermit needs a rope strong enough to tow a 3,000-pound boat trailer. The neighbor, who isn't in the rope business, picks a rope from the garage and sells it to Kermit for $20. The rope snaps. Which implied warranty, if any, did the neighbor make?
o: None, because the neighbor isn't a merchant.
Fitness for a particular purpose, because the seller knew the purpose and that Kermit relied on the choice.
None, because the sale was under $500.
