Merchantability, because the neighbor sold goods for value.
Both merchantability and fitness.
oe: Fitness doesn't require a merchant.
Correct. § 2-315 applies to any seller with reason to know the purpose and the buyer's reliance.
Price is irrelevant to warranties.
Merchantability requires a merchant for goods of that kind.
No merchantability warranty, since the neighbor isn't a merchant.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Fitness from a non-merchant

q: A contract calls for weekly deliveries to Herry's Gym on Mondays. For two months, Herry accepts Friday deliveries without complaint. Herry then writes the seller: "From now on, deliveries must arrive on Monday, as the contract says." The seller has not changed its position in reliance on the Friday schedule. Must the seller deliver on Mondays going forward?
o: Yes, but only if Herry pays for the change.
No, because a waiver is permanent once made.
Yes, because Herry may retract the waiver by reasonable notice.
No, because two months of silence modified the contract under § 2-209(1).
No, because the Friday deliveries became a course of performance that modified the contract.
oe: No consideration is needed to retract.
Waivers can be retracted for future performance.
Correct. § 2-209(5). The seller hasn't materially changed position, so retraction isn't unjust.
Silence isn't agreement to modify.
Course of performance can show a waiver, but a waiver of an executory term can be retracted.
topic: 4 · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Retracting a waiver

q: A coffee roaster agrees to buy all its requirements of green beans from an importer, with an estimate of 10,000 pounds a year. The roaster honestly lands a national grocery account and now needs 60,000 pounds. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The contract is void, because the roaster's needs changed.
The importer must supply 60,000 pounds, because the estimate was only a good-faith guess.
The importer must supply all 60,000 pounds, because the roaster acted in good faith.
The importer must supply 60,000 pounds but may charge the market price for the excess.
None of the above.
oe: Changed needs don't void the contract.
An estimate isn't just a guess; it limits the quantity that can be demanded.
Good faith isn't the only limit.
§ 2-306 limits quantity; it doesn't reprice the excess.

Correct. The importer need not supply a quantity unreasonably disproportionate to the estimate, even though the roaster acted in good faith. Disproportion is a separate limit (§ 2-306(1); Orange & Rockland; Problem 4-2). No choice says that.
topic: 7 · Quantity & price — Good faith but disproportionate

q: A furniture maker agreed to buy its requirements of oak from a mill, with an estimate of 40,000 board feet. A recession cuts its furniture orders in half, and it orders only 18,000 board feet. The mill sues. What is the furniture maker's best argument?
o: Decreases are never limited under § 2-306.
The estimate was only a guess and binds no one.
Requirements contracts lack mutuality of obligation.
Its orders fell for a genuine reason, so it acted in good faith.
The mill can resell the oak to other buyers at the market price, so it has suffered no damages.
oe: Some courts apply both tests to decreases, and all apply good faith.
Estimates matter under § 2-306(1).
Good faith supplies the obligation.
Correct. A real lack of orders can be good faith (Problem 4-1(c)), and many courts test decreases only for good faith.
That goes to damages, not to whether the buyer breached.
topic: 7 · Quantity & price — Requirements: honest decrease

q: A Vermont furniture maker contracts to deliver custom tables to Abby's restaurant in Burlington. Abby assigns the right to receive the tables to a restaurant in Honolulu, which demands delivery there. Must the furniture maker deliver to Honolulu?
o: Yes, if the Honolulu restaurant agrees to pay the extra shipping cost of getting the tables there.
No, because the assignment would materially change and increase the seller's burden.
No, because buyers can never assign their rights.
Yes, because rights are freely assignable.
None of the above.
oe: The seller's duty would still change materially.
They usually can.
Not when the assignment materially changes the other party's duty.
B is correct.
topic: 13 · Assignment & delegation — Assignment that increases burden

q: At a garage sale, Rowlf sells Scooter a used kayak. Scooter pays, and Rowlf says, "It's on the dock out back. Grab it whenever today." Before Scooter returns that afternoon, the kayak is stolen. Who bears the loss?
o: Rowlf, because Scooter never received the kayak.
Rowlf, because theft isn't a casualty.
Scooter, because Scooter paid in full.
Scooter, because Rowlf tendered it.
Rowlf, because the kayak was still on Rowlf's property.
oe: Receipt is the test only for a merchant seller.
Theft is a casualty to the goods.
Payment isn't the trigger; tender is.
Correct. § 2-509(3). Rowlf put the kayak at Scooter's disposition and told Scooter where it was.
Location doesn't decide it.
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — Non-merchant seller: tender

q: A distributor properly terminates an at-will supply arrangement. Before termination, the supplier shipped a load of nonconforming goods that the distributor accepted. What happens to the distributor's claim for that load?
o: It survives, because termination ends only executory duties.
It survives only if the distributor reserved it in the notice.
It becomes a claim for lost profits.
It is extinguished, because termination discharges all obligations.
None of the above.
oe: No reservation is needed.
It stays a claim for the earlier breach.
Only executory obligations.
A is correct.
topic: 14 · Termination — What survives termination

q: Gonzo's signed email to Rizzo says: "Confirming you will buy 80 cases of olive oil at $40 per case." The parties actually agreed on $45 per case. Rizzo seeks to enforce the deal against Gonzo. Is the email sufficient under § 2-201(1)?
o: Yes, because a record isn't insufficient just because it misstates a term other than quantity.
No, because an email can't be signed.
No, because Rizzo did not sign it.
No, because it misstates the price.
Yes, but the contract is enforceable only at the $40 price stated in the email, not the $45 actually agreed.
oe: Correct. § 2-201(1). The statute caps quantity only; the true price is proved at trial.
A typed name in an email is a signature, and an email is a record.
It must be signed by the party to be charged, Gonzo.
A misstated term other than quantity doesn't make a record insufficient.
The statute of frauds doesn't fix the price. The parties prove the actual terms.
topic: 3 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Misstated price

q: Zoe buys a new e-bike. The manufacturer's warranty, in a sealed booklet inside the box that Zoe couldn't see before paying, limits remedies to repair and excludes consequential damages in bold capitals. The motor fails, and five repair attempts never fix it. What is the most likely result?
o: The exclusion is enforceable, because it was printed in bold capitals.
The repair remedy failed of its essential purpose, and the exclusion, tested separately, is likely unconscionable because Zoe couldn't see it before buying.
The repair remedy failed, so the consequential-damages exclusion automatically falls with it.
The repair remedy hasn't failed, because the manufacturer is still trying.
Zoe is limited to more repair attempts, because the remedy was expressly exclusive.
oe: Clear type doesn't help if the buyer couldn't see the term before buying.
Correct. This tracks Razor v. Hyundai: two separate tests ("concentric walls"), and a preprinted consumer exclusion unavailable before the sale was unconscionable.
That's the dependent approach (Adams), which Razor rejected.
Repeated failed repairs are the classic failure of essential purpose.
An exclusive remedy that fails of its essential purpose gives way to general remedies (§ 2-719(2)).
topic: 11 · Remedies & remedy limitations — Hidden consumer exclusion

q: The Count mails a written offer to buy 300 pewter figurines. The offer says nothing about how to accept. The seller accepts by text message the day the offer arrives. The Count argues that a mailed offer can be accepted only by mail. Is there a contract?
o: No, because a text message is not a signed record.
No, because acceptance must use the same medium as the offer.
Yes, but only if the seller also mails a confirmation.
Yes, because any reasonable medium of acceptance will do.
None of the above.
oe: Acceptance doesn't have to be signed; signatures matter for the statute of frauds.
The UCC rejects that rule.
No second acceptance is needed.
Correct. § 2-206(1)(a), unless the offer unambiguously says otherwise.
D is correct.
topic: 2 · Formation — Medium of acceptance

q: A contract requires Abby to tell a sign maker by March 1 which colors to use for 40 signs. Abby gives no specifications until April 15, and the sign maker couldn't start without them. Which statement is correct?
o: Abby may cancel because the signs were late.
The contract is void, because a material term (the colors) was left open and never agreed by the deadline.
The sign maker is excused for the delay and may proceed reasonably or treat Abby's failure as a breach.
The sign maker is in breach for missing the delivery date.
None of the above.
oe: Abby caused the delay.
The parties agreed Abby would specify.
Its delay was caused by Abby.
C is correct.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — Failure to cooperate

q: Short on cash, Guy Smiley "sells" a fleet of delivery vans to a lender for $200,000 and must buy them back in one year for $230,000. Guy keeps using the vans the whole time. Which law most likely governs the deal?
o: Article 2, but the buyback clause is unenforceable.
Article 9, because it is really a secured loan.
Article 2A, because Guy keeps possession like a lessee.
The common law of contracts, because no goods change hands.
Article 2, because the parties called the deal a sale.
oe: Article 2 doesn't govern a disguised security interest at all.
Correct. § 2-102(3)(a): a "sale" with a mandatory repurchase at a higher price is a disguised security interest, governed by Article 9.
Nothing here is a lease. Guy owes a fixed repayment, which is how a loan works.
The vans are goods. The question is which article governs the transaction.
The label doesn't control. A mandatory buyback at a higher price is a loan in substance.
topic: 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Disguised security interest

q: Fozzie buys a used food truck from a dealer. When Fozzie picks it up two days after signing, the dealer says, "By the way, the engine was rebuilt last year." It wasn't. How strong is Fozzie's claim that the statement was an express warranty?
o: Weak, because Fozzie couldn't have relied on it when deciding to buy.
Strong, but only if the dealer knew the statement was false.
Weak, because the statement came after the contract and Fozzie gave nothing new for it.
Weak, because oral statements can't be express warranties.
Strong, because a post-sale statement can be a warranty without new consideration.
oe: Cmt. 7 lets a post-sale statement become part of the deal.
Warranty liability doesn't depend on the seller's knowledge.
Consideration isn't needed for a modification (§ 2-209(1)).
They can.
Correct. § 2-313 cmt. 7.
topic: 5 · Express warranties — Statement at delivery

q: Bert, a guitar dealer, contracts to sell Ernie a specific 1959 guitar, to be picked up Saturday. On Friday night, Bert leaves a space heater running next to the guitar, and the guitar is destroyed in the resulting fire. Is Bert excused?
o: No, because Bert must deliver a substitute guitar.
Yes, because a fire is beyond the parties' control.
Yes, because the guitar was unique and identified.
No, because Bert's negligence is fault.
None of the above.
oe: Bert can't, and the remedy is damages.
Bert's negligence caused this fire.
The loss must also be without fault.
Correct. § 2-613 requires the loss to occur without fault; negligence is fault (Problem 6-6(a)'s coffee pot).
D is correct.
topic: 16 · Excuse from performance — Casualty caused by negligence

q: For six months a buyer accepts cheese deliveries every other week, although the contract requires weekly deliveries. Relying on that pattern, the seller sells one of its two trucks and signs a long-term route plan built on the every-other-week schedule. The buyer now demands weekly deliveries starting next week. What is the most likely result?
o: The buyer may insist, but must pay for the seller's new truck.
The buyer may insist, because a waiver can always be retracted.
The buyer may insist, because the contract has no NOM clause.
The seller is excused from all further deliveries.
None of the above.
oe: If retraction is unjust, it fails. There's no pay-to-retract rule.
Not when retraction would be unjust because of a material change of position.
The NOM clause doesn't matter to whether a waiver can be retracted.
Nothing excuses the seller entirely.

Correct. § 2-209(5): a waiver can't be retracted if retraction would be unjust because the other party materially changed position in reliance. Selling a truck and committing to a route plan likely qualifies. No choice says that.
topic: 4 · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Retraction blocked by reliance

q: A contract for industrial pumps says: "Any action for breach must be brought within 6 months after delivery." The buyer discovers a defect and sues 10 months after delivery. What result?
o: The suit is barred, because merchants may agree to any period they like.
The suit is barred, because parties may set any limitations period.
The suit is timely, because the limitations period can never be shortened.
The suit is timely, because the period can't be cut below one year.
None of the above.
oe: The one-year floor applies to merchants too.
They can't go below one year.
It can be, to as little as one year.
D is correct.
topic: 11 · Remedies & remedy limitations — Shortened limitations period

q: At a bike shop, Ernie picks out a specific red bicycle on the showroom floor and signs a contract to buy it, agreeing to pick it up next week after the shop adds a bell. When is the bicycle identified to the contract?
o: When the contract is made, because it is a sale of existing goods already identified.
When Ernie pays the full price.
When the shop tenders the bicycle to Ernie.
When the shop finishes adding the bell.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. § 2-501(1)(a). Ernie also gets an insurable interest then.
Payment doesn't control identification.
Identification comes earlier.
The bicycle was already identified.
A is correct.
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — Identification

q: A used-car dealer sells Waldorf a 10-year-old sedan with 140,000 miles. Two months later, it needs new brake pads, a normal wear item at that age. Waldorf claims breach of the implied warranty of merchantability. What result?
o: Waldorf wins, because the dealer is a merchant for used cars.
Waldorf wins, because any repair needed within 90 days is a breach.
Waldorf wins, because a dealer's car must be fit for ordinary driving.
The dealer wins, because used goods carry no implied warranty.
None of the above.
oe: Merchant status triggers the warranty but doesn't prove breach.
No such rule.
It must be fit at the level appropriate for a car of that age and mileage.
Used goods can carry the warranty.

Correct. The dealer likely wins: the merchantability warranty covers used goods only at the quality appropriate for goods of that age and use, and worn brake pads on a 140,000-mile car are normal. No choice says that.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Used goods

q: Herry and a supplier orally agree on 300 dumbbells. The supplier's signed confirmation, which Herry is suing on, mistakenly lists 200. The supplier refuses to deliver any. How many dumbbells can Herry enforce against the supplier?
o: 300, if Herry proves the oral agreement.
None, because the record misstates the quantity.
None, unless the supplier admits the deal in court.
300, because a record isn't insufficient merely because it misstates a term.
None of the above.
oe: The contract isn't enforceable beyond the quantity in the record.
The record is still sufficient. It just caps enforcement.
The signed record is sufficient up to the quantity it shows.
That's true of other terms. A misstated quantity limits enforcement to the quantity shown.
Correct. Herry can enforce 200: § 2-201(1) says the contract is not enforceable beyond the quantity shown in the record. No choice says 200.
topic: 3 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Quantity cap

q: Zoe orders 50 red umbrellas for prompt shipment. Out of red, the seller ships 50 blue umbrellas with a note: "Out of red. Sending blue as an accommodation in case these help." Zoe does not want them. What are Zoe's rights?
o: Zoe must pay for them unless Zoe returns them within ten days.
Zoe may keep them at the price agreed for the red umbrellas.
Zoe may reject them and sue for breach, because the shipment accepted the order with nonconforming goods.
Zoe may reject them, and the seller hasn't breached, because the shipment was only a counteroffer.
Zoe must keep them, because the shipment accepted Zoe's order.
oe: No rule makes Zoe pay for a counteroffer Zoe never accepted.
There is no contract for blue umbrellas unless Zoe accepts the counteroffer.
That's the result without an accommodation notice. Here the seller gave one.
Correct. § 2-206(1)(b): shipping nonconforming goods is not an acceptance if the seller seasonably notifies the buyer that it's an accommodation.
The accommodation notice keeps the shipment from being an acceptance.
topic: 2 · Formation — Accommodation with notice

q: Rowlf contracts to sell Scooter a specific vintage piano. Before risk passes, a flood damages the piano's finish without fault of either party, though the piano still plays. What are Scooter's options?
o: Scooter may accept the piano and sue Rowlf for the full cost of refinishing.
The contract is automatically avoided.
Scooter must take the piano at the full price.
Scooter may avoid the contract and recover the cost of a comparable piano.
None of the above.
oe: Accepting with an allowance ends any further claim.
Only a total loss avoids it automatically.
Scooter may avoid or take it with an allowance.
Avoidance gives no damages; Rowlf isn't in breach.

Correct. On a partial loss, Scooter may inspect and either treat the contract as avoided or accept the piano with a price allowance, with no further claim against Rowlf (§ 2-613(b)). No choice says that.
topic: 16 · Excuse from performance — Partial loss

q: A seafood distributor has supplied fish to Miss Piggy's restaurant for three years under an oral arrangement with no stated term. The distributor gives two months' notice that it will stop, explaining only that it wants to focus on grocery stores. Miss Piggy argues that the termination is invalid. Which of the following is correct?
o: It is invalid, because the statute of frauds requires written notice of termination.
It is invalid, because the distributor needs a good-faith reason that benefits both parties.
It is invalid, because a contract that has lasted three years can be ended only for cause.
It is invalid, because good faith requires the distributor to offer new terms first.
None of the above.
oe: The statute of frauds doesn't govern termination notices.
No reason is required.
Duration doesn't convert it into a for-cause arrangement.
Good faith imposes no such duty.
Correct. The termination is valid: an indefinite contract may be terminated at any time with reasonable notice, and no reason is needed (§ 2-309(2)-(3); Santa Fe). Two months is likely reasonable.
topic: 14 · Termination — No reason needed

q: A sawmill agrees to sell its entire output of wood chips to a paper company at a fixed price. The sawmill's costs rise, so it loses money on every ton. It shuts down its chip line solely to stop those losses, though it still has plenty of logs and lumber orders. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The shutdown is a breach only if the paper company covers.
The shutdown is in good faith, because a seller need not keep operating a line that loses money on every ton.
The shutdown is fine, because output contracts set no minimum.
The shutdown is likely in bad faith, because cutting losses alone doesn't justify it.
None of the above.
oe: Cover is a remedy, not an element of breach.
Merely curtailing losses isn't a good-faith reason under § 2-306.
Good faith limits reductions.
Correct. A shutdown for lack of orders can be good faith; one merely to cut losses isn't (cmt. 2).
D is correct.
topic: 7 · Quantity & price — Output: shutdown to cut losses

q: Statler and Waldorf sign a contract for 50 theater seats stating the price, quantity, and delivery date. It has no merger clause and was meant to be final on the terms it covers, but not a complete statement of the deal. Waldorf offers evidence that, before signing, they orally agreed that Statler would also bolt the seats to the floor. Is the evidence admissible?
o: Yes, but only if the installation term was in writing.
No, because installing the seats contradicts the written delivery term, which says nothing about installation.
Yes, because it's a consistent additional term and the writing isn't complete.
No, because prior oral agreements are never admissible.
None of the above.
oe: Oral consistent terms can come in too.
It adds to the deal; it doesn't negate any written term.
Correct. § 2-202(b).
Consistent additional terms can come in when the writing isn't complete.
C is correct.
topic: 12 · Parol evidence rule — Partial integration: consistent term

q: A used-equipment dealer sells Big Bird a forklift under a signed contract that says, in large bold capitals, "SOLD AS IS." It doesn't mention merchantability or fitness. The forklift's hydraulics fail the next week. Which implied warranties, if any, did the dealer disclaim?
o: Merchantability only, because "as is" is about ordinary quality.
All warranties, including the warranty of title.
None, because a disclaimer of merchantability must mention merchantability by name, and this one doesn't.
Merchantability and fitness, because "as is" excludes implied warranties.
Only fitness, because a fitness disclaimer needn't mention fitness.
oe: It reaches fitness too.
"As is" doesn't disclaim title (§ 2-312(2)).
"As is" is an exception to the magic-word rule.
"As is" reaches both implied quality warranties.
topic: 10 · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — "As is"

q: At a yard sale, Bert tells a shopper that a used espresso machine "works great. I used it this morning." The shopper pays $60, and the machine fails the first time the shopper uses it. Did Bert make an express warranty?
o: Yes, because every statement a seller makes about the goods during the sale is an express warranty.
Yes, but only the implied warranty of merchantability.
No, because the sale was under $500.
No, because Bert is not a merchant.
Probably yes, because it states a fact about the machine's present condition.
oe: Opinion, commendation, and value statements aren't.
Bert isn't a merchant, and the question is about an express warranty.
The price affects the statute of frauds, not warranties.
Any seller can make an express warranty.
Correct. Statements of present working condition are close calls from a casual seller (Petti), but "I used it this morning" makes this one specific and factual.
topic: 5 · Express warranties — Casual seller's statement

q: Elmo sells a used gaming console to Zoe through an online marketplace for $350. Neither is a merchant. The console never works. Does Article 2 govern the sale?
o: Yes, because Article 2 applies to transactions in goods whatever the parties' status.
Yes, but only the provisions that apply between merchants.
No, because the price is under $500.
No, because the marketplace, not Elmo, is the seller.
No, because Article 2 applies only when at least one party to the sale is a merchant in goods of that kind.
oe: Correct. Scope never depends on merchant status. (Because Elmo isn't a merchant, though, Elmo gives no implied warranty of merchantability.)
It's the reverse: some provisions apply only to merchants, and the rest apply to everyone.
$500 is the statute-of-frauds threshold (§ 2-201), not a limit on Article 2's scope.
Elmo transferred the console for a price, so Elmo is the seller.
Article 2 reaches consumer-to-consumer sales (Problem 1-4).
topic: 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Scope: consumer to consumer

q: A shipment contract for 1,000 pounds of coffee says nothing about when payment is due. The seller ships and demands payment the moment the coffee is handed to the carrier. Unless the parties agree otherwise, when must the buyer pay?
o: When the seller hands the coffee to the carrier.
Within 30 days of the invoice date.
When and where the buyer receives the coffee.
Before the seller ships.
Whenever the seller reasonably demands.
oe: That's when risk passes in a shipment contract, not when payment is due.
The Code presumes no credit.
Correct. § 2-310(a), even when the seller is authorized to ship.
Not the default.
No such rule.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — When payment is due

q: Rosita contracts to deliver 1,000 standard paper-towel rolls to a school. Rosita delegates delivery to another supplier, which delivers defective rolls. The school sues Rosita. What result?
o: Rosita is liable only if the school objected to the delegation.
Rosita isn't liable, because the duty was validly delegated.
The school may sue only the new supplier.
Rosita is liable only for the cost of the rolls, not other damages.
None of the above.
oe: Objection isn't required.
Delegation doesn't release the delegator.
It may sue Rosita.
Rosita is liable for breach as if Rosita had performed.
Correct. Rosita is liable: delegating performance doesn't relieve the delegating party of its duty or of liability for breach (§ 2-210(1)). No choice says that.
topic: 13 · Assignment & delegation — Delegator stays liable

q: A nursery agrees to deliver 40 trees to Big Bird's yard in the nursery's own truck. The contract has no shipping or risk terms. On the way, a storm topples a tree onto the truck and destroys the cargo. Who bears the loss?
o: The nursery, but only if it was negligent.
Big Bird, because the trees had been identified to the contract.
Big Bird, because the nursery tendered the trees by loading them.
Big Bird, because the trees were delivered to a carrier.
None of the above.
oe: Risk of loss doesn't depend on fault.
Identification doesn't pass risk.
Loading its own truck isn't a tender to the buyer.
The seller's own truck isn't a carrier.
Correct. The nursery bears it. Its own truck isn't a carrier, so § 2-509(3) applies, and a merchant seller keeps the risk until the buyer receives the goods (Problem 4-6(a)). No choice says that.
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — Seller's own truck

q: A bottling plant buys a filling machine under a negotiated contract that limits remedies to repair and excludes consequential damages. Repeated repairs fail, and the plant loses $400,000 in profits. Under the majority, independent approach, can the plant recover its lost profits?
o: No, because the plant's only remedy is more repairs.
Yes, because consequential-damages exclusions are always unconscionable.
No, unless the exclusion is unconscionable, which is unlikely in a negotiated commercial deal.
Yes, because once the repair remedy fails of its essential purpose, every limit tied to it falls as well.
None of the above.
oe: The failed repair remedy gives way to general remedies, minus the excluded damages.
Only consumer personal-injury exclusions are prima facie unconscionable.
Correct. The independent approach (Chatlos, Razor) tests the exclusion separately under § 2-719(3); commercial-loss exclusions between merchants are usually fine.
That's the dependent approach.
C is correct.
topic: 11 · Remedies & remedy limitations — Independent approach: commercial

q: Grover and Elmo orally agree that Elmo will sell Grover a used sound system for $350. Before delivery, they orally agree to add speakers and raise the price to $700. Elmo later refuses to deliver the speakers. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The modification is enforceable, because the original contract didn't need a writing.
The modification fails without a signed record, since the new deal is $500 or more, but the $350 deal stands.
The original contract is discharged, so Elmo owes nothing.
Neither deal is enforceable, because once the parties raised the price, the whole contract fell within the statute of frauds.
The $700 deal is enforceable, because modifications need no consideration.
oe: What matters is the contract as modified.
Correct. § 2-209(3) applies the statute of frauds to the contract as modified (Problem 3-4(a)). The failed modification may still operate as a waiver.
A failed modification doesn't discharge the original contract.
The original $350 deal survives.
Consideration isn't the problem. The statute of frauds is.
topic: 4 · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Modification and the SOF

q: Rizzo buys a new dishwasher from an appliance store. On its third cycle it floods the kitchen. No one can identify the exact defect, and Rizzo used it normally. What is Rizzo's best argument for breach of merchantability?
o: The store was negligent in choosing the model.
The store had reason to know Rizzo's particular purpose.
Any product that fails within its first year of normal household use is unmerchantable as a matter of law.
An early failure under normal use is circumstantial proof that the dishwasher was defective when sold.
Rizzo doesn't have to prove anything once a merchant sells the goods.
oe: Negligence isn't required.
Washing dishes is the ordinary purpose.
Too broad.
Correct. Problem 3-10's mower that fails on its fourth use: early failure, absent misuse, supports an inference of a defect at the time of sale.
Rizzo must still show breach.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Early failure as proof

q: Waldorf asks a cabinetmaker to build custom shelves and invites acceptance by starting work. The cabinetmaker begins building but never tells Waldorf. Six weeks later, having heard nothing, Waldorf hires someone else. The cabinetmaker sues. What result?
o: Waldorf wins, because an offer can be accepted only by a return promise.
Waldorf wins, because Waldorf was never notified and may treat the offer as lapsed.
The cabinetmaker wins, because beginning performance accepted the offer.
The cabinetmaker wins, because the shelves are specially manufactured goods that the cabinetmaker had substantially begun.
None of the above.
oe: Under § 2-206, beginning performance can be a reasonable mode of acceptance.
It can, but the offeror must be notified within a reasonable time.
That is a statute-of-frauds exception, not a rule of acceptance.
B is correct.
topic: 2 · Formation — Acceptance by beginning performance

q: While selling Kermit a used lathe, a machinery dealer says aloud: "Understand there's no warranty of merchantability on this one, and it isn't guaranteed fit for any particular job." The written contract says nothing about warranties. Which implied warranties were effectively disclaimed?
o: Fitness only, because merchantability disclaimers must be written.
Neither, because every disclaimer must be in a conspicuous writing.
Both, because the dealer clearly told Kermit about each warranty before the sale, and Kermit agreed.
Merchantability only, because a fitness disclaimer must be in writing.
None of the above.
oe: Merchantability disclaimers may be oral.
Only a written merchantability disclaimer must be conspicuous.
A fitness disclaimer must be in writing.
D is correct.
topic: 10 · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Oral disclaimers

q: When Grover asks whether a used canoe has ever been damaged, the seller replies, "Never. The hull is original and has never been patched." The seller later testifies that it never meant to give a warranty. The hull had been patched. Is there an express warranty?
o: No, because the seller never said "warrant" or "guarantee."
No, because Grover could have inspected the hull before buying.
No, because the seller lacked any intent to warrant.
Yes, but only if Grover had the canoe inspected.
None of the above.
oe: No formal words are required.
A buyer's chance to inspect doesn't erase an affirmation of fact.
Intent isn't required.
Inspection isn't a condition of the warranty.

Correct. There is an express warranty. § 2-313(2) needs no formal words like "warrant" and no specific intent; an affirmation of fact about the goods, made in answer to Grover's question, is part of the basis of the bargain. No choice says that.
topic: 5 · Express warranties — No intent or magic words

q: Which of the following oral contracts is enforceable without any signed record?
o: A $600 sale of a painting at an art fair.
A $5,000 sale of a boat between two individuals.
A $900 sale of office chairs that the buyer later refuses to accept.
A $480 sale of a used bicycle between neighbors.
All of the above.
oe: Over $500, with no record or exception.
Over $500, and no exception appears.
Over $500, and nothing was received and accepted.
Correct. The statute of frauds reaches only sales for $500 or more.
Only D is under $500.
topic: 3 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — $500 threshold

q: A hardware store sells Ernie a can of paint labeled "Eggshell White." The paint inside is bright yellow but otherwise high quality. Which merchantability requirement does the paint most clearly fail?
o: Fitness for Ernie's particular purpose.
Fair average quality for fungible goods.
Fitness for the ordinary purposes for which paint is used.
Conformity to the promises or affirmations of fact on the container or label.
None of the above.
oe: That's § 2-315, not merchantability, and no particular purpose appears.
The quality is high.
It paints well.
D is correct.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Merchantability: label

q: While researching an Article 2 question, Kermit's lawyer finds an Official Comment that seems to say something different from the enacted text of the section. Which approach is correct?
o: Follow the comment unless a court in the same state has rejected it.
Follow whichever reading better promotes uniformity among the states.
Follow the comment, because the legislature adopted it as the authoritative interpretation.
Treat the section as void for ambiguity and apply the common law instead.
Follow the text, because the comments help interpret the Code but are not law.
oe: The text controls without any need for a contrary case.
Policy is a last-resort tiebreaker, not a way to override the text.
In most states the comments are not enacted. They are an aid, not law.
Ambiguity calls for interpretation, not displacement of the Code.
Correct. The comments are the most important interpretive aid, but the text controls when they conflict.
topic: 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Official Comments vs. text

q: A town commissions a well-known sculptor to create a bronze statue for its square. Without the town's consent, the sculptor hands the work to an apprentice. May the town refuse the apprentice's statue?
o: Yes, because the town has a substantial interest in having the original promisor perform.
Yes, because delegation is never allowed for specially made goods.
No, because duties under a sales contract are freely delegable.
No, if the apprentice's statue matches the design.
None of the above.
oe: Standard specially made goods can be delegated.
Not where the other party has a substantial interest in the original promisor's performance.
The town bargained for the sculptor's work.
A is correct.
topic: 13 · Assignment & delegation — Substantial interest in the promisor

q: A contract limits a buyer's remedy for a defective industrial dryer to "replacement of defective parts." A defect causes a fire that destroys the whole dryer. What is the buyer's best argument?
o: The clause never applies to fires.
The clause is unenforceable because it wasn't conspicuous.
The limited remedy failed of its essential purpose, so general UCC remedies are available.
The clause is a penalty.
None of the above.
oe: Nothing in the clause excludes fires.
Remedy limits needn't be conspicuous.
Correct. § 2-719(2). Replacement parts are useless when the machine is gone (Problem 5-7).
Penalty analysis applies to liquidated damages, not remedy limits.
C is correct.
topic: 11 · Remedies & remedy limitations — Failure of essential purpose

q: A feed store contracts to sell Snuffy 200 bags of a standard brand of chicken feed. Before delivery, a flood destroys the store's entire stock of that feed without the store's fault. Which statement is correct?
o: Snuffy must pay for the destroyed feed, because it was being held for Snuffy.
The store is excused under § 2-615, because a flood is an unforeseeable event.
Snuffy may avoid the contract or accept the damaged feed with a price allowance.
The contract is avoided under § 2-613, because the goods were destroyed without fault.
None of the above.
oe: Risk hadn't passed to Snuffy.
Losing its own stock of a widely available product doesn't make performance impracticable.
That's § 2-613(b), which doesn't apply to unidentified fungible goods.
§ 2-613 covers only goods identified when the contract was made.
Correct. The store isn't excused. The feed is fungible and wasn't identified when the contract was made, so § 2-613 doesn't apply, and the store must still tender 200 bags from another source.
topic: 16 · Excuse from performance — Fungible goods destroyed

q: A grain elevator has contracts to buy 40,000 bushels of soybeans from a farm, which keeps postponing delivery. The market then shifts so that further postponement would cost the elevator heavily, the state attorney general publicly questions whether contracts like these are legal, and the farm stops returning the elevator's calls. The elevator writes demanding, as assurance, that the farm post a letter of credit for its hedging losses and sign a promise to deliver. Is the demand proper?
o: Yes, because a party may demand any assurance it wants once grounds exist.
No, because asking for a letter of credit demands more than the contract required, which is itself a repudiation.
Yes, because the grounds were reasonable and the demand wasn't unreasonable as a matter of law.
No, because grounds for insecurity must come from the farm's own conduct.
None of the above.
oe: The demand must seek only adequate assurance.
Every demand for assurance asks for more than the original promise; that alone isn't repudiation (§ 2-610 cmt. 2).

Correct. This is Top of Iowa v. Sime Farms: the inverted market, the attorney general's statement, and the farmer's silence gave reasonable grounds, and margin or a letter of credit plus a delivery promise was a permissible demand.
Grounds are objective and can come from the market or third parties.
C is correct.
topic: 15 · Insecurity & repudiation — Grounds from the market and a regulator

q: Gonzo orders a crate of tools "C.O.D." When the carrier arrives, Gonzo demands to open the crate and inspect before paying. The carrier refuses. Who is right?
o: The carrier, because under a C.O.D. term the buyer isn't entitled to inspect before paying.
Gonzo, because a buyer may always inspect before paying.
Gonzo, because paying is acceptance.
The carrier, because inspection before payment is never allowed when goods are shipped by a carrier.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. § 2-513(3)(a). Payment still isn't acceptance (§ 2-512(2)).
Not when the contract calls for C.O.D.
Payment isn't acceptance.
Normally the buyer may inspect after arrival.
A is correct.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — C.O.D.: no inspection first

q: A signed contract for industrial lubricant says it is "the complete and exclusive statement of the terms of the agreement." The buyer offers (1) evidence of a trade usage that suppliers give 60 days' notice before discontinuing a grade, and (2) evidence that the seller orally promised before signing to give such notice. Which is admissible to supplement the contract?
o: Both.
Neither, because the writing is complete and exclusive.
Only (1), because usage of trade can supplement even a complete and exclusive writing, but a prior promise cannot.
Only (2), because the promise was made specifically to this buyer.
None of the above.
oe: The prior oral promise can't supplement a complete and exclusive writing.
Usage of trade can still supplement it.
Correct. § 2-202(a) and (b); Problem 5-12(a) and (b).
It's barred by the full integration.
C is correct.
topic: 12 · Parol evidence rule — Complete writing: usage vs. prior promise

q: In the restaurant-supply trade, sellers do not customarily season new cast-iron pans before delivery. Under three earlier contracts, however, Gonzo's Cookware always delivered seasoned pans to Miss Piggy's bistro. Their newest contract says nothing about seasoning, and Gonzo delivers unseasoned pans. Is Gonzo in breach?
o: Yes, because of course of dealing.
No, because usage of trade does not require seasoning.
Yes, because of course of performance.
No, because course of dealing can never add a term to a written contract.
No, because the contract's express terms say nothing about seasoning.
oe: Correct. Prior conduct between the parties establishes a common understanding that supplements the agreement (§ 1-303(b), (d)).
Course of dealing prevails over usage of trade (§ 1-303(e)).
Course of performance is conduct under this contract. The earlier contracts are course of dealing.
It can supplement even a written contract (§ 2-202(a)).
Silence isn't a contradiction. Course of dealing supplements the terms.
topic: 4 · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Course of dealing

q: Rowlf grants a distributor the exclusive right to sell Rowlf's pianos in three states. The contract says nothing about how hard the distributor must work. For a year, the distributor makes no effort to market the pianos. Which statement is correct?
o: Rowlf's only remedy is to terminate without notice.
The distributor owes best efforts to promote sales.
The distributor must buy a reasonable quantity even if it can't resell them.
The distributor has no duty to sell, because the contract is silent.
The contract is void for lack of a quantity term.
oe: Rowlf can claim breach.
The duty is best efforts to promote sales, not a quantity purchase.
The Code implies one.
Exclusive dealing contracts are enforceable.
topic: 7 · Quantity & price — Exclusive dealing

q: A contract says: "Seller will ship the generators to Buyer's warehouse in Ohio; Seller pays freight." It says nothing else about risk. The carrier's train derails, destroying the generators. Who bears the loss?
o: The buyer, but only if the buyer insured the generators.
The seller, because it agreed to pay freight to Ohio.
The buyer, because risk passed when the seller delivered the generators to the carrier.
The carrier alone, so neither party bears it.
The seller, because the contract names the buyer's Ohio warehouse as the place the generators were going.
oe: Insurance doesn't decide who bears the risk.
Paying freight doesn't make it a destination contract.
Correct. § 2-509(1)(a). Only an express undertaking to bear the risk in transit makes a destination contract.
One party bears the risk and can pursue the carrier.
Naming a destination doesn't either.
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — Shipment contract presumption

q: A Vermont glassworks agrees to make custom stained-glass panels and have them "properly crated and delivered to" a church construction site in Georgia. It crates them properly and hands them to a trucking company. The truck crashes on the highway, shattering the panels. The church refuses to pay. Who bears the loss?
o: The glassworks, because "delivered to" made this a destination contract.
The church, because "delivered to" doesn't overcome the shipment-contract presumption, so risk passed at the carrier.
The glassworks, because custom goods stay at the seller's risk until installed.
The trucking company alone, so the church owes nothing until it collects.
None of the above.
oe: "Delivered to" doesn't overcome the shipment-contract presumption.
Correct. This is Windows v. Jordan Panel (Problem 4-7(a)). The church must pay and can pursue the carrier.
No special rule for custom goods.
The buyer owes the price; its claim against the carrier is separate.
B is correct.
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — "Delivered to" the site

q: A court finds a clause in a consumer installment contract unconscionable. Which of the following may the court NOT do under § 2-302?
o: Limit the clause's application to avoid an unconscionable result.
Enforce the rest of the contract without the clause.
Refuse to enforce the whole contract.
Let the parties present evidence of the clause's commercial setting and purpose.
Award the buyer punitive damages for the seller's overreaching.
oe: It may.
It may.
Correct. § 2-302 lets a court refuse to enforce, strike, or limit. It is a defense, not a source of damages.
topic: 3 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Unconscionability: remedies

q: A contract says: "Seller will repair or replace any defective part." It says nothing more about remedies. The goods are defective, and the buyer sues for damages under § 2-714 without first asking for repair. Is the buyer limited to repair or replacement?
o: No, because repair remedies are unenforceable.
No, because it isn't expressly exclusive.
Yes, because the parties agreed on repair or replacement.
Yes, because a buyer must always give the seller a chance to repair.
None of the above.
oe: They're enforceable when properly agreed.
An agreed remedy is optional unless expressly exclusive.
No general duty to accept repair.
B is correct.
topic: 11 · Remedies & remedy limitations — Agreed remedy: optional

q: Kermit signs a contract to buy a tractor after the seller threatens to spread false rumors that would ruin Kermit's business unless Kermit signs. Article 2 says nothing about duress. What law decides whether Kermit can avoid the contract?
o: No law, because Article 2 occupies the whole field of sales of goods.
The common law of duress, which supplements the Code.
The law of the state where the tractor was made.
Article 2's unconscionability section, the Code's only policing doctrine.
Federal law, because a threat to ruin a business is a federal tort.
oe: Article 2 doesn't displace general contract doctrines it doesn't address.
Correct. § 1-103(b) lists duress, coercion, fraud, mistake, and other validating and invalidating causes as supplementing the UCC.
Where the goods were made doesn't choose the governing law.
§ 2-302 is one tool, not the only one, and duress is a separate doctrine.
Nothing makes this a federal question.
topic: 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Common law supplements: duress

q: A seller's 12-page form contract disclaims "all implied warranties, including merchantability" in paragraph 31, in the same small type as everything else, under the heading "Miscellaneous." Is the merchantability disclaimer effective?
o: Yes, because the buyer signed the contract.
Yes, because it mentions merchantability.
It depends on whether a jury finds it conspicuous.
No, because merchantability can be disclaimed only orally.
No, because it isn't conspicuous.
oe: Signing doesn't make fine print conspicuous.
A written disclaimer must also be conspicuous.
Conspicuousness is a question for the court.
It may be disclaimed in writing if conspicuous.
topic: 10 · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Conspicuous

q: Herry buys a ladder from a hardware store and lends it to a coworker, who uses it at the coworker's own home. The ladder collapses and injures the coworker. Under which § 2-318 alternative can the coworker sue the store for breach of warranty?
o: Alternative A only.
Alternative B only.
Alternatives B and C, but not A.
All three alternatives.
None of them, because the coworker isn't in privity with the store.
oe: Alternative A covers only the buyer's family, household, and guests in the buyer's home.
B covers the coworker, but so does C.

Correct. B covers any natural person who may reasonably be expected to use the goods and is injured in person; C covers any person reasonably expected to be affected who is injured. A doesn't reach a coworker at the coworker's home.
A doesn't cover the coworker.
§ 2-318 extends warranties beyond the buyer.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Privity: borrowed ladder

q: The contract between Rowlf's Pianos and a wood supplier says the price "includes delivery." In the lumber trade, delivery is usually billed separately. The supplier bills Rowlf for delivery anyway. Who wins?
o: The supplier, because Rowlf should have known the usage.
Neither, because the conflict makes the price term too indefinite.
Rowlf, because express terms control over an inconsistent usage of trade.
Rowlf, but only if Rowlf was unaware of the usage.
The supplier, because usage of trade supplements every contract in that trade, including this one.
oe: Knowledge of the usage doesn't beat an express term.
The express term is clear.
Correct. § 1-303(e): express terms prevail over course of performance, course of dealing, and usage of trade.
Rowlf wins either way.
It supplements terms; it doesn't override them.
topic: 4 · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Express term vs. usage of trade

q: Kermit and a lumber yard trade calls and emails but never agree on every term. The yard delivers lumber, Kermit uses it, and Kermit pays half the invoice. Kermit now argues that no contract was ever formed. What is the best response?
o: A contract exists only for the half of the lumber Kermit paid for.
No contract exists, because acceptance must mirror the offer.
No contract exists, because no one can say when the contract was made.
A contract exists, because conduct can show agreement.
No contract exists, because the parties never agreed on all material terms.
oe: That mixes in the part-performance exception to the statute of frauds. The question is formation.
The UCC rejects the mirror-image rule.
§ 2-204(2): a contract can exist even if the moment of its making is undetermined.
Correct. § 2-204(1). Delivery, use, and partial payment show agreement.
That is the common-law view. Open terms don't defeat a UCC contract (§ 2-204(3)).
topic: 2 · Formation — Formation by conduct

q: A contractor building a steel water tank for a developer hears that the developer's financing may fall through. The contractor writes that it will continue only if the developer's owner personally guarantees payment, the developer escrows the full price, or the developer sells the contractor a share of the project. Which statement best describes the demand?
o: It is improper only because it wasn't sent within 30 days of the rumors.
It is proper, because the rumors gave reasonable grounds for insecurity.
It is proper, because each option gives the developer a choice.
It is improper, because these demands go beyond adequate assurance.
None of the above.
oe: The 30 days runs for the response, not the demand.
Grounds don't justify an excessive demand.
Every option goes beyond adequate assurance.
Correct. This is PDM v. Brookhaven: demands like a personal guarantee, escrow, or an ownership stake were more than adequate assurance as a matter of law.
D is correct.
topic: 15 · Insecurity & repudiation — Excessive demand

q: A fuel supplier's costs double after a surge in crude oil prices, and it now loses money on a fixed-price contract with Fozzie's trucking fleet. The supplier claims commercial impracticability. What result?
o: No, because higher costs alone don't excuse.
The supplier is excused, but must give Fozzie 30 days' notice.
The supplier is excused, because performance has become unprofitable.
The supplier is excused if the increase exceeds 50%.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. § 2-615 cmt. 4: rising costs and market swings are the risks a fixed-price contract covers.
It isn't excused at all.
Unprofitability isn't impracticability.
No percentage rule.
A is correct.
topic: 16 · Excuse from performance — Higher costs

q: A signed written contract, intended as final, states a price of $12,000 for a delivery van. The buyer offers evidence that the day before signing, the seller orally agreed to $10,000. Is the evidence admissible to prove a $10,000 price?
o: Yes, if the buyer proves the oral deal by clear and convincing evidence.
No, because it would contradict a final written term.
No, but only if the writing has a merger clause.
Yes, because oral agreements control over printed forms.
Yes, if the writing is only a partial integration.
oe: The rule bars the evidence regardless of its strength.
Correct. § 2-202 (first clause).
No merger clause is needed to bar contradiction of a final term.
No such rule.
Even a partial integration can't be contradicted.
topic: 12 · Parol evidence rule — Contradictory prior term

q: A dealer tells Herry, "This vintage guitar will be worth twice what you're paying within five years." It isn't. Herry sues for breach of express warranty. What result?
o: Herry loses, because the statement was oral.
Herry wins, because the dealer is an expert, so the statement is a warranty.
Herry wins if Herry relied on the statement.
Herry loses; it's an affirmation of value.
Herry wins, because the statement was specific and measurable.
oe: Oral statements can be warranties.
Expertise doesn't turn a prediction of value into a warranty.
Reliance can't turn a statement of value into a warranty.
Correct. § 2-313(2) excludes affirmations merely of the value of the goods.
It's specific, but it concerns value, which the Code excludes.
topic: 5 · Express warranties — Affirmation of value

q: Rizzo pays a lab $1,200 to test a shipment of food-grade oil, finds it contaminated, and rightfully rejects it. Who bears the cost of the test?
o: Rizzo, because the buyer always bears inspection costs.
The seller, but only if the contract says so.
Rizzo, unless the contract expressly shifts the cost.
The parties split it.
None of the above.
oe: Only if the goods conform or aren't rejected.
The Code shifts the cost without a contract term.
The Code shifts it.
No splitting rule.
Correct. The seller bears it: the buyer bears inspection costs but recovers them from the seller if the goods don't conform and are rejected (§ 2-513(2)). No choice says that.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — Inspection costs

q: A contract says: "Buyer may not assign this contract." The buyer assigns its right to receive the goods to a subsidiary but keeps the duty to pay. Is the assignment a breach?
o: No, because a ban on assigning "the contract" bars only delegation.
No, because anti-assignment clauses are void under the UCC.
Yes, because a buyer's right to receive goods is never assignable.
Yes, because the clause bars any assignment of the contract, including an assignment of the buyer's rights.
None of the above.
oe: They can bar delegation.
It often is.
A ban on assigning "the contract" is read narrowly.
A is correct.
topic: 13 · Assignment & delegation — Ban on assigning "the contract"

q: A hospital agrees to buy "all the surgical gloves it needs this year" from a supplier at a fixed price. Midyear, the supplier refuses to deliver, arguing that the contract is unenforceable because it states no quantity. What is the most likely result?
o: The supplier wins, because the hospital never promised to buy any minimum amount.
The supplier wins, because a contract with no stated quantity is too indefinite.
The hospital wins, but only for gloves already ordered.
The supplier wins, because requirements contracts are illusory.
None of the above.
oe: Good faith limits the buyer's requirements, which supplies mutuality.
A requirements term is a quantity term.
The contract is enforceable for the year.
§ 2-306 rejects that view.
Correct. The hospital wins: a requirements term measures quantity by the buyer's actual good-faith requirements (§ 2-306(1)), so the contract is neither indefinite nor illusory. No choice says that.
topic: 7 · Quantity & price — Requirements: not too indefinite

q: A seller ships fragile ceramic lamps to Telly under a shipment contract but packs them loosely in a single box with no padding. They arrive smashed from ordinary handling. Who bears the loss?
o: Telly, unless Telly inspected the packing before shipment.
Telly, because risk passed when the lamps were given to the carrier under the shipment contract.
The carrier, because the lamps broke while it had them.
The seller, because its failure to make a reasonable shipping arrangement caused the loss.
None of the above.
oe: The buyer has no duty to inspect the packing.
Not when the seller's improper shipment caused the loss.
The carrier isn't liable for damage caused by the shipper's own packing.
D is correct.
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — Bad packing causes the loss

q: Bunsen's lab accepts a late delivery of glassware in January without comment. In October, having said nothing to the seller in the meantime, Bunsen sues for damages caused by the delay. What is the seller's best defense?
o: The claim is barred by the four-year statute of limitations.
Bunsen should have rejected the delivery instead.
Bunsen's claim is barred because Bunsen never gave timely notice of the breach.
Bunsen waived all damages for the delay by accepting the late delivery without objecting at the time.
None of the above.
oe: Ten months is well within four years.
Bunsen could accept and still claim damages, with timely notice.
Correct. § 2-607(3)(a): a buyer who accepts must notify the seller of breach within a reasonable time after discovering it or be barred from any remedy.
Accepting goods doesn't waive damages for the breach (§ 2-607(2)).
C is correct.
topic: 4 · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Notice after accepting a late delivery

q: Which fact points MOST strongly toward treating a seller's statement as puffing rather than an express warranty?
o: The statement was general and hedged, and the seller volunteered it without being asked.
The seller made the statement in answer to the buyer's specific question about the goods' performance.
The seller knew far more about the goods than the buyer.
The statement was written into the contract.
The statement could be measured or checked.
oe: Correct. General, equivocal, volunteered statements look like puffing.
That points toward a warranty.
That points toward a warranty.
Written statements lean toward warranties (though writing isn't decisive).
That points toward a warranty.
topic: 5 · Express warranties — Factors: puffing

q: Two weeks after signing a complete and exclusive contract to buy 100 tents, Fozzie and the seller orally agree to change the color from green to tan. The contract has no NOM clause. The seller later argues that the parol evidence rule bars proof of the change. Is the seller right?
o: Yes, because the change was oral.
Yes, because the writing is complete and exclusive.
No, because color is never a material term.
Yes, because a NOM clause is implied in every complete and exclusive writing.
None of the above.
oe: Oral modifications are fine absent a NOM clause or a statute-of-frauds problem (and only quantity must be in the record).
That bars prior and contemporaneous terms, not later ones.
Materiality isn't the reason.
No clause is implied.
Correct. The seller is wrong: the parol evidence rule never bars evidence of agreements made after the writing; that's modification, governed by § 2-209. No choice says that.
topic: 12 · Parol evidence rule — Later agreement

q: Waldorf's supplier learns from trade sources that Waldorf has paid several other suppliers months late, though Waldorf has paid this supplier on time. May the supplier demand adequate assurance?
o: No, because only a missed payment under this contract creates insecurity.
No, because trade reports are never reasonable grounds.
Yes, and it may cancel immediately without waiting for a response.
No, because Waldorf has never breached this contract.
None of the above.
oe: Grounds are broader than that.
They can be, judged by commercial standards.
It must wait a reasonable time (up to 30 days) for assurance.
Grounds needn't come from this contract.
Correct. Yes: grounds for insecurity are objective and need not arise from the contract at issue; late payments to others can be reasonable grounds (§ 2-609 cmt. 3). No choice says that.
topic: 15 · Insecurity & repudiation — Grounds outside this contract

q: A defective space heater that Snuffy buys sets fire to the bakery next door, damaging the bakery's ovens but injuring no one. The bakery sues the heater's seller for breach of warranty. Under which § 2-318 alternative is the bakery most likely covered?
o: Alternative B, because the bakery's owner is a natural person.
Alternative A, because the bakery was affected by the heater.
Any of the three, because a seller can't exclude § 2-318.
Alternative C, which isn't limited to personal injury.
None, because property damage is never recoverable for breach of warranty.
oe: B is limited to persons injured in person.
A covers only the buyer's family, household, and home guests, and only for personal injury.
True that it can't be excluded, but the alternatives differ in whom they cover.
Correct. Alternative C isn't limited to personal injury.
Property damage can be a consequential loss (§ 2-715(2)(b)).
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Privity: property damage

q: A spice importer contracts to sell saffron from a single named region to three restaurants. A government embargo unexpectedly cuts off that region, leaving the importer only 40% of what it needs. Which statement best describes the importer's obligations?
o: It is not excused, because embargoes are always foreseeable.
It is excused only to the extent of the shortfall, must allocate fairly among customers, and must notify them seasonably.
It is fully excused and may deliver nothing to anyone.
It must fill one restaurant's order completely before the others.
None of the above.
oe: An unexpected embargo cutting off the agreed source can excuse.
Correct. § 2-615(b)-(c). Each buyer may then take its share or terminate (§ 2-616).
Only to the extent of the shortfall.
It must allocate fairly.
B is correct.
topic: 16 · Excuse from performance — Embargo: allocation

q: A space-heater maker's warranty excludes "all consequential damages, including for personal injury." A defect in a heater bought for home use burns Elmo's hand, and Elmo sues for the medical bills. Is the exclusion enforceable as to those damages?
o: Yes, if the exclusion was conspicuous.
No, because consequential damages can't be excluded for any breach.
Yes, because consequential damages may always be excluded.
No, because limiting damages for personal injury from consumer goods is prima facie unconscionable.
None of the above.
oe: Conspicuousness doesn't cure prima facie unconscionability.
Commercial-loss exclusions are generally fine.
Not if the exclusion is unconscionable.
D is correct.
topic: 11 · Remedies & remedy limitations — Personal injury exclusion

q: Gonzo signs a contract to buy a commercial pizza oven from Animal. The contract states the model and price but says nothing about the delivery date, the place of delivery, or when payment is due. Which statement best describes the contract?
o: It is enforceable, but only by the party that did not draft it.
It is an agreement to agree that neither party can enforce.
It fails for indefiniteness, because delivery, place, and payment timing are material terms the parties never settled.
It is enforceable if the parties intended to contract and there is a reasonably certain basis for giving a remedy.
It is enforceable only after the parties agree on the missing terms.
oe: No such rule exists.
Intent to contract plus a basis for a remedy is enough.
Under the UCC, open terms don't defeat a contract.
Correct. § 2-204(3). Gap fillers supply the place (§ 2-308), time (§ 2-309), and payment (§ 2-310).
The gap fillers supply them.
topic: 2 · Formation — Open terms

q: Ernie's restaurant-supply company in Delaware contracts to buy espresso machines from a manufacturer in Italy. The contract says nothing about governing law. Which body of law most likely governs the sale?
o: The CISG, because the parties are in different countries, unless they agree otherwise.
Article 2A, because the machines are commercial equipment.
The common law of contracts, because Article 2 cannot reach a seller located outside the United States.
UCC Article 2, because the buyer is located in Delaware.
Italian law, because the seller makes the goods.
oe: Correct. The third factor is the parties' location; an international sale of goods falls under the CISG unless the parties' agreement (the fourth factor) displaces it.
Article 2A governs leases. This is a sale.
The CISG, not the common law, fills that role for international sales.
The location factor points the other way: the parties are in different countries.
Where the goods are made doesn't decide it.
topic: 1 · The UCC & which law governs — International sale

q: Snuffy agrees to buy 300 bales of hay from a farmer, "price to be agreed at delivery." Both intend to be bound. At delivery, they can't agree on a price. What price governs?
o: The farmer's asking price, because the seller sets open prices.
The average of the parties' last offers.
A reasonable price at the time for delivery.
The market price at the time of contracting.
No price, because price is an essential term.
oe: Not unless the contract lets the seller fix it.
No such rule.
Correct. § 2-305(1)(b). Compare Problem 4-3(a).
The measure is a reasonable price at the time for delivery.
The parties intended to be bound.
topic: 7 · Quantity & price — Price left to agreement

q: Gonzo, a seller, assigns to Rizzo "all my rights under my contract with Kermit." Rizzo accepts. Rizzo then fails to deliver. Can Kermit sue Rizzo?
o: No, because Kermit isn't a party to the assignment.
Yes, because Rizzo's acceptance is a promise to perform that Kermit can enforce.
Yes, but only if Kermit consented to the assignment.
No, because the assignment transferred only Gonzo's rights under the contract, not any of Gonzo's duties to Kermit.
None of the above.
oe: § 2-210(5) lets the other party enforce it.
Correct. § 2-210(5); Problem 6-2(c).
Consent isn't required.
"All my rights" also delegates the duties.
B is correct.
topic: 13 · Assignment & delegation — "All my rights": assignee's promise

q: A buyer receives a shipment of 100 office chairs. Which of the following would NOT be an acceptance of the chairs?
o: Bolting the chairs to an auditorium floor after noticing torn fabric.
Reselling ten of the chairs to an employee.
Keeping the chairs for a reasonable time to inspect and test them.
Failing to reject after a reasonable chance to inspect.
Telling the seller it will keep the chairs despite a defect.
oe: Also an act inconsistent with the seller's ownership.
An act inconsistent with the seller's ownership (§ 2-606(1)(c)).
Correct. Possession during a reasonable inspection isn't acceptance (§ 2-606(1)).
Acceptance under § 2-606(1)(b).
Acceptance under § 2-606(1)(a).
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — Not an acceptance

q: Before buying a used pickup, Oscar inspects it carefully and sees the tailgate is badly dented. Oscar later discovers that the transmission has a hidden defect that no ordinary inspection would reveal. Which implied-warranty claims does Oscar's examination bar?
o: Neither, because examination never affects implied warranties.
Only the tailgate claim.
Both, because Oscar examined the truck before buying.
Only the transmission claim, because hidden defects are excluded.
None of the above.
oe: It does, as to discoverable defects.
Examination excludes only what it ought to have revealed.
It's the reverse.
B is correct.
topic: 10 · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Examination

q: In a freely negotiated three-year supply contract, Kermit agreed to buy cocoa at a fixed price that matched the market at the time. Two years later, cocoa prices collapse, and the fixed price is now triple the market. Kermit argues the price term is unconscionable. What result?
o: Kermit loses, because the term was fair when made.
Kermit wins, because a court may rewrite any price term that becomes unfair.
Kermit wins if a jury finds the price shocking.
Kermit loses, because merchants can never claim unconscionability.
Kermit wins, because the term is now substantively oppressive.
oe: Correct. Unconscionability is judged at the time of contracting, and nothing here was procedurally or substantively unfair then.
Courts don't rewrite bargains for later market changes. Kermit bore that risk.
The court decides unconscionability as a matter of law.
Merchants can raise it, though rarely successfully.
Later events don't count. Unconscionability is judged when the contract is made.
topic: 3 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Unconscionability: when judged

q: Elmo, a dentist, sells a used road bike to Telly through a classified ad, saying, "The frame is carbon fiber." The frame is aluminum. Telly sues for breach of express warranty, and Elmo argues that a non-merchant can't make a warranty. What result?
o: Telly wins, because any seller can make an express warranty.
Elmo wins, because only merchants make warranties under Article 2.
Elmo wins, because the bike is used.
Elmo wins, because Telly could have checked the frame.
Telly wins, but only under the implied warranty of merchantability.
oe: Correct. § 2-313 applies to every seller.
Only merchantability requires a merchant.
Used goods can carry express warranties.
A buyer's chance to inspect doesn't erase a specific affirmation of fact.
Elmo isn't a merchant, so no merchantability warranty arises.
topic: 5 · Express warranties — Express warranty by a non-merchant

q: A fuel supply contract lets the seller set the monthly price but adds: "A price no higher than the published regional index plus 3 cents a gallon is conclusively in good faith." Is the clause effective?
o: Yes, because parties may set standards for good faith that are not manifestly unreasonable.
Yes, because the parties may disclaim the duty of good faith entirely, as long as they do so expressly.
No, because the duty of good faith can't be varied by agreement.
No, because price terms set by one party are void.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. § 1-302(b). Tying the price to an objective index is the kind of standard Problem 5-1(a) suggests.
Good faith can never be disclaimed.
It can't be disclaimed, but the parties may set standards for measuring it.
§ 2-305(2) allows a price set by one party.
A is correct.
topic: 4 · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Setting good-faith standards

q: Worried by reports that a buyer is struggling, a seller phones the buyer and says it will stop shipping until it gets "some kind of assurance." The seller never puts the demand in writing and halts shipments. Has the seller acted properly?
o: Yes, because the seller had reasonable grounds for insecurity.
Yes, because a phone call is a sufficient demand between merchants.
Yes, because suspension is allowed whenever a party feels insecure.
No, because sellers may never suspend shipments.
None of the above.
oe: Grounds alone don't justify suspending without a written demand.
§ 2-609(1) requires a written demand.
Only after a written demand.
They may, after a proper demand.

Correct. No: a party may suspend its performance only after demanding adequate assurance in writing (or another record). Halting shipments on an oral demand risks the seller's own breach. No choice says that.
topic: 15 · Insecurity & repudiation — Demand must be written

q: A complete and exclusive contract calls for "Grade A" maple lumber but doesn't define the term. The buyer offers evidence that in the furniture trade, "Grade A" means knot-free boards. Is the evidence admissible?
o: No, unless the court first finds that "Grade A" is ambiguous on the face of the written contract.
No, because the writing is complete and exclusive.
Yes, because usage of trade may explain the terms of even a complete and exclusive writing.
Yes, but only if the seller agrees.
None of the above.
oe: Some courts require that for other explanatory evidence, but not for usage, dealing, or performance.
Usage of trade can explain even a complete writing.
Correct. § 2-202(a). Cmt. 1(c): no prior finding of ambiguity is needed for usage evidence.
Admissibility doesn't depend on consent.
C is correct.
topic: 12 · Parol evidence rule — Usage explains a term

q: Before selling Zoe a used boat, the seller says, "Please have it hauled out and inspected before you buy." Zoe declines. Afterward, Zoe finds a soft spot in the hull that any haul-out inspection would have revealed. Which statement is correct?
o: The seller's demand disclaimed all warranties, express and implied.
Zoe keeps the implied-warranty claim, because Zoe never actually inspected.
Zoe's claim survives unless the seller also said "as is."
Zoe keeps the claim, because the seller's demand was oral.
None of the above.
oe: It affects only implied warranties, and only for discoverable defects.
Refusing after the seller's demand counts.
The refusal is an independent ground.
The demand need not be written.

Correct. Zoe has no implied-warranty claim for that defect: when a buyer refuses to examine after the seller's demand, there is no implied warranty as to defects an examination ought to have revealed (§ 2-316(3)(b)). No choice says that.
topic: 10 · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Refusal to examine

q: A buyer's purchase order says "F.O.B. Buyer's warehouse." The seller's acknowledgment, a definite acceptance, says "F.O.B. Seller's plant." Both are merchants, and neither objects. The goods are destroyed in transit. Under the knockout rule applied in Daitom, which statement is correct?
o: The loss is split, because neither form controls.
The seller bears the loss, because the acceptance's different term is a proposal the buyer never accepted.
The buyer bears the loss, because both terms drop out and the default is a shipment contract.
The seller bears the loss, because the offer's term controls.
None of the above.
oe: The gap filler, not a split, fills the hole the conflicting terms leave.
Some courts treat different terms that way, but the question asks about the knockout rule.
Correct. The different terms cancel (cmt. 6), the gap filler applies, and a contract is presumed to be a shipment contract, so risk passed on delivery to the carrier (§ 2-509(1)(a)).
Under the knockout rule, neither form's term controls.
C is correct.
topic: 2 · Formation — Knockout: shipping terms

q: A print shop agrees to print and bind 2,000 cookbooks for Miss Piggy's restaurant. Most of the price reflects printing and binding labor rather than paper and ink. The books arrive with pages bound upside down. Under the predominance factors (amended § 2-102, cmt. 3), how is the transaction best characterized?
o: Goods predominate, because manufacturing labor counts toward the goods.
It cannot be characterized until a court applies the gravamen test.
Services predominate, because labor makes up most of the price.
Services predominate, because printing is a skilled trade.
It is a license of intellectual property, because the books contain recipes.
oe: Correct. Cmt. 3: manufacturing services count toward goods; design services don't. Compare Problem 1-2.
The gravamen test is a different approach, and the predominance factors answer the question here.
Labor used to manufacture goods counts toward the goods, not against them.
Skill doesn't change the analysis. Manufacturing labor counts toward goods.
Miss Piggy is buying printed books, not rights in the recipes.
topic: 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Hybrid: manufacturing services

q: Prairie Dawn signs and sends a purchase order for 1,000 notebooks at $2 each to a stationery wholesaler. The wholesaler never signs anything but ships. Before the notebooks arrive, Prairie Dawn tries to cancel, arguing that the wholesaler never signed. Can the wholesaler enforce the contract against Prairie Dawn?
o: Yes, but only if the wholesaler sends a confirmation within ten days.
No, because both parties must sign a record.
No, because the goods have not yet been received and accepted.
No, because the wholesaler's shipment is not a signed record.
None of the above.
oe: No confirmation is needed.
Only the party against whom enforcement is sought must sign.
That exception isn't needed when there's a signed record.
The wholesaler doesn't need a record signed by itself to enforce against Prairie Dawn.
Correct. Yes: the record need be signed only by the party against whom enforcement is sought, and Prairie Dawn signed the order. No choice says that.
topic: 3 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Signed by the party charged

q: Two merchants negotiate a contract for a custom bakery oven, delivery by September 1. Because lost sales would be hard to prove, they set liquidated damages of $800 a day of delay, based on their talks about the bakery's expected profits. The oven arrives 20 days late, but the bakery's actual losses are only $2,000. Is the $16,000 clause enforceable?
o: Likely yes, because it was reasonable in light of the anticipated harm.
Yes, because parties may agree to any amount.
No, because liquidated-damages clauses must be conspicuous.
No, because $16,000 is eight times the bakery's actual loss, which makes the clause a penalty.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. § 2-718(1) ("anticipated or actual harm"); Problem 5-6.
An unreasonably large amount is a void penalty.
They needn't be.
The test asks about anticipated or actual harm.
A is correct.
topic: 11 · Remedies & remedy limitations — Liquidated damages: anticipated harm

q: Oscar buys a vintage jukebox from Elmo with a check that later bounces. Before Elmo finds out, Oscar sells the jukebox to Zoe, who pays fair value and knows nothing about the check. Elmo sues Zoe to recover it. Who wins?
o: Zoe, because Oscar had voidable title and could pass good title to a good-faith purchaser for value.
Zoe, but only if Zoe is a merchant.
Elmo, because a buyer who pays with a check that bounces gets void title and can pass nothing to anyone.
Elmo, because Oscar never paid for the jukebox.
Elmo, unless Zoe has had the jukebox for more than ten days.
oe: Correct. § 2-403(1)(b): a buyer whose check is dishonored has voidable title.
A good-faith purchaser for value need not be a merchant.
Void title is a thief's. A dishonored check gives voidable title.
Oscar still got voidable title.
No such rule.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Voidable title: bad check

q: A seller assigns its right to payment under a $20,000 contract to a bank, and the bank notifies the buyer. The buyer pays the seller anyway, and the seller disappears with the money. What is the buyer's position?
o: The buyer is discharged unless the bank sues within ten days.
The buyer owes the bank only half.
The buyer is discharged, because the bank should have collected from the seller.
The buyer is discharged, because it paid the party it contracted with.
None of the above.
oe: No such rule.
No splitting rule.
The risk of paying the wrong party after notice is on the buyer.
After notice, payment to the assignor doesn't discharge.
