Correct. The buyer still owes the bank: once notified of the assignment, the obligor must pay the assignee (Problem 6-2(a)). No choice says that.
topic: 13 · Assignment & delegation — Paying the assignor after notice

q: A collector agrees to sell a rare stamp collection to a dealer under a signed memo saying, "We will not be bound until we agree on a price." The dealer pays a $5,000 deposit and receives part of the collection. They never agree on a price. What is the effect?
o: A reasonable price applies, because the parties signed a memo and partly performed, showing intent to contract.
There is no contract, so each side returns what it received (or pays its value).
The dealer must pay whatever price the collector names in good faith.
The collector may keep the deposit as liquidated damages.
None of the above.
oe: They expressly intended not to be bound without an agreed price.
Nothing gave the collector the power to set the price.
There's no contract and no liquidated-damages term.
B is correct.
topic: 7 · Quantity & price — No deal without a price

q: A seller ships 200 cases of canned soup to Gonzo under a shipment contract on pallets slightly below trade standard. A train strikes the truck and destroys everything; the packing played no role. Who bears the loss?
o: Gonzo, because the packing didn't cause the loss.
The seller, because its packing breached § 2-504.
The parties split it, because both bear some fault.
The seller, because any nonconformity keeps risk on the seller.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Problem 4-7(d)(2) and Windows v. Jordan Panel: the packing must cause the loss before risk shifts back.
A § 2-504 failure shifts risk only if it causes material delay or loss.
Gonzo bears no fault, and there's no splitting rule.
Not where the nonconformity didn't cause the loss.
A is correct.
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — Bad packing, unrelated loss

q: A city power plant signs a 15-year contract to buy natural gas at a fixed price with annual escalators. Five years in, gas prices collapse, and the plant could buy power far more cheaply elsewhere. The plant claims its performance is excused. What result?
o: The plant is excused by frustration of purpose.
The plant is excused, because the escalators make the price unreasonable.
The plant is excused by commercial impracticability.
No, because a fixed price puts the risk of a falling market on the buyer.
None of the above.
oe: Its purpose (generating power) can still be achieved.
It agreed to the escalators.
Paying more than the market isn't impracticability.
Correct. NIPSCO v. Carbon County Coal: a buyer that misforecasts the market "has only himself to blame."
D is correct.
topic: 16 · Excuse from performance — Fixed price, falling market

q: Kermit buys a matched set of eight dining chairs sold only as a set. One chair has a cracked leg. Kermit wants to keep seven and reject the cracked one. May Kermit do so?
o: No, because the defect is too minor to justify any rejection.
No, because accepting part of a commercial unit accepts the whole unit.
Yes, but only if the seller agrees to cure.
Yes, because a buyer may accept any units and reject the rest when a delivery fails to conform in any respect.
None of the above.
oe: The perfect tender rule allows rejection.
Correct. §§ 2-601(c), 2-606(2). Kermit may reject or accept the whole set.
Cure doesn't change the commercial-unit rule.
Any commercial units, and the set is one commercial unit.
B is correct.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — Commercial unit

q: Grover and a supplier trade a draft contract marked "DRAFT: FOR DISCUSSION," with blanks for price and delivery date. Neither signs it. In a later dispute, the supplier argues that the draft bars evidence of their earlier discussions. Is the supplier right?
o: Yes, because Grover had a chance to object to the draft.
No, because a draft isn't a final expression.
Yes, because the draft is a written record of the deal.
No, because unsigned writings are always inadmissible.
None of the above.
oe: The question is whether it was intended as final.
Correct. An unfinished draft is outside § 2-202.
It's not a final expression.
The draft may be admissible as evidence; it just doesn't trigger the parol evidence rule.
B is correct.
topic: 12 · Parol evidence rule — Draft writing

q: Inside the sealed box of a stand mixer that Miss Piggy buys, a printed insert says, "Motor rated for 30 minutes of continuous kneading." Miss Piggy reads it only after getting home. The motor burns out after ten minutes of kneading. Can the insert's statement be an express warranty?
o: Yes, but only if the statement is conspicuous.
No, because statements packed in a box are never part of the contract.
No, because a motor rating is the manufacturer's opinion.
Yes, because inserts and manuals can be part of the basis of the bargain even if read after the sale.
No, because Miss Piggy read the insert only after the sale, so it could not have been part of the bargain.
oe: Conspicuousness matters for disclaimers, not for creating warranties.
They can be.
A rating is specific and measurable, an affirmation of fact.
Correct. The outline notes that owner's manuals and package inserts can create warranties even when read later (and cmt. 7 treats post-sale statements as possible modifications).
Statements first read after the sale can count.
topic: 5 · Express warranties — Package insert

q: Telly's contract with a printer has a NOM clause. Telly casually tells the printer that a later delivery date "should be fine." Without asking for a signed change, the printer turns down other work to meet the new date. If Telly sues for late delivery, why is the printer's estoppel argument weak?
o: Estoppel is not available under the UCC.
Estoppel requires a signed record.
Estoppel requires a signed record showing the promise the printer relied on.
The NOM clause makes it less reasonable to rely on an unwritten change.
None of the above.
oe: It is. § 1-103(b) preserves estoppel.
Estoppel rests on reliance, not on a writing.
It turned down other work.
Correct. Estoppel needs reasonable, detrimental reliance. A NOM clause undercuts the reasonableness of relying on an oral change (Problem 3-5(C)).
D is correct.
topic: 4 · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Estoppel and a NOM clause

q: A single-delivery contract calls for 1,000 blue mugs. The seller delivers 1,000, but 20 have a slightly lighter blue glaze. The delivery deadline has passed, and the seller had no reason to think the shipment would be acceptable. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The buyer must give the seller a further reasonable time to cure.
The buyer may reject all, accept all, or accept some commercial units and reject the rest.
The buyer may reject only the 20 mugs and must keep the rest.
The buyer must accept, because the nonconformity is insubstantial.
The buyer may reject only if the lighter glaze substantially impairs the value of the whole shipment.
oe: That applies only if the seller reasonably believed the tender would be acceptable (§ 2-508(2)).
Correct. § 2-601. No right to cure remains: the time has passed and the seller had no reason to believe the tender would be accepted (§ 2-508).
The buyer may also reject or accept the whole.
The perfect tender rule doesn't require substantial impairment.
That's the installment-contract standard.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — Perfect tender

q: In January, a lumber mill agrees to sell Big Bird's Builders 50 truckloads a month for the year at $300 a load, a price set when the market was weak. By June, a housing boom has pushed market prices to $500, and the mill is losing money on every load. The mill tells Big Bird it will stop shipping entirely unless Big Bird agrees to $450. Unable to find lumber elsewhere, Big Bird signs the new price, then later sues to recover the difference. What is the most likely result?
o: Big Bird wins, because price increases are never valid modifications.
Big Bird wins, because the mill got the increase by threatening to breach, which is not honesty in fact.
The mill wins, because a modification needs no consideration.
Big Bird wins, because the mill gave no new consideration.
The mill wins, because the market shift gave it a legitimate commercial reason to ask for more, so it acted in good faith.
oe: They can be, if sought in good faith.
Correct. Like Sharon Steel in Roth Steel, the mill had an objective reason, but extracting the change with a threat to stop performing is bad faith (§ 2-209 cmt. 2).
True (§ 2-209(1)), but a modification must still be sought in good faith.
§ 2-209(1) abolishes the consideration requirement.
That satisfies only the objective part of good faith.
topic: 4 · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Modification extracted by threat

q: A contract to sell a $3,000 used copier says that if the buyer fails to take delivery, the buyer must pay the seller $25,000. The seller's realistic loss from a buyer's breach would be a few hundred dollars. What is the likely status of the clause?
o: It is void as a penalty, because the amount is unreasonably large.
It is enforceable, because the buyer agreed to it.
It is void, because liquidated damages aren't allowed in consumer sales.
It is enforceable, but only up to the contract price.
None of the above.
oe: Agreement doesn't save a penalty.
They're allowed if reasonable.
Courts don't rewrite penalties; they strike them.
A is correct.
topic: 11 · Remedies & remedy limitations — Liquidated damages: penalty

q: Rosita leaves a vintage watch for repair at a jewelry store that also sells used watches. The jeweler sells it to the Count, who buys in the ordinary course without knowing Rosita owns it. Who has the better claim to the watch?
o: The Count, because possession is nine-tenths of the law.
Rosita, because the watch was entrusted only for repair.
Rosita, because a buyer from a repair shop can't get better title than the shop had.
Rosita, because the jeweler had no title to transfer.
None of the above.
oe: Not the rule. The Count wins under § 2-403(2).
The purpose of the entrustment doesn't matter (§ 2-403(3)).
Entrustment is the exception to that rule.
Entrustment gives the merchant power to transfer the entruster's rights even without title.

Correct. The Count wins: entrusting goods to a merchant who deals in goods of that kind gives the merchant power to transfer all the entruster's rights to a buyer in ordinary course (§ 2-403(2)). No choice says that.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Entrustment: repair shop that sells

q: At regional cattle auctions, it is well established that animals are sold with no warranty of health beyond what the seller announces. Snuffy buys a heifer at such an auction; no announcement is made. The heifer is sick. Does Snuffy have a claim for breach of the implied warranty of merchantability?
o: No, because livestock are not goods.
Yes, because no one mentioned merchantability.
Yes, because usage of trade can only add warranties, not remove them.
Yes, because a disclaimer must be in a conspicuous writing.
No, because an implied warranty can be excluded by course of dealing, course of performance, or usage of trade.
oe: Animals are goods.
The magic-word rule isn't the only way to disclaim.
It can exclude them too.
Not for exclusion by usage of trade.
topic: 10 · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Usage of trade disclaimer

q: A contractor orders custom drainage fittings designed solely for a city stormwater project. Before delivery, the city cancels the project, and the fittings have no other use. The contractor claims it is excused. What is its best argument?
o: Casualty to identified goods under § 2-613.
Frustration of purpose, because both parties assumed the project would go forward.
Commercial impracticability under § 2-615, because the city's cancellation was an unforeseen contingency.
The statute of frauds, because the contract was oral.
None of the above.
oe: The fittings weren't destroyed.
Correct. § 1-103(b) brings in common-law frustration; § 2-615 cmt. 9 notes a buyer may be excused when a contract is tied to a specific venture (Problem 6-8(a)).
That's a seller's argument, and nothing about cost is in the facts.
Nothing says it was oral.
B is correct.
topic: 16 · Excuse from performance — Frustration of purpose

q: A propane wholesaler requires its franchised dealers to buy propane at a price the wholesaler sets. The price is within the range competitors charge, but internal memos show the wholesaler set it to drive the dealers out so it could run the outlets itself. The dealers sue under § 2-305(2). Which statement best describes the law?
o: The dealers win only if the price exceeded every competitor's price.
The dealers lose, because § 2-305 does not apply to franchise agreements.
Under Mathis, the motive can show bad faith despite a market price, but most courts hold a commercially reasonable price is in good faith whatever the motive.
The dealers win everywhere, because a price set by one party must equal the lowest market price.
The dealers lose everywhere, because any price within the posted market range is in good faith.
oe: Mathis held a price within the competitive range could still be in bad faith.
Mathis applied it to franchise dealers' purchases.
Correct. Mathis upheld a bad-faith verdict on similar facts; Shell v. HRN and Autry v. BP (the majority) reject motive-based review of a commercially reasonable, non-discriminatory price.
No court requires the lowest price.
Under Mathis, an improper motive takes the case out of the safe harbor.
topic: 7 · Quantity & price — Price set to squeeze out buyers

q: A seller assigns its right to payment to a factoring company, which notifies the buyer. The goods turn out to be defective, and the buyer has a $4,000 warranty claim. The factor demands the full price. What may the buyer do?
o: Nothing; it must pay the full price and sue the seller.
Assert its warranty claim against the factor, because an assignee takes subject to the buyer's defenses.
Refuse to pay anything, because the assignment was a breach.
Pay the seller instead.
None of the above.
oe: The buyer keeps its defenses against the assignee.
Correct. The assignee steps into the assignor's shoes.
Assigning a right to payment isn't a breach.
After notice, it must pay the assignee.
B is correct.
topic: 13 · Assignment & delegation — Assignee takes subject to defenses

q: Oscar orally agrees to buy Snuffy's vintage motorcycle for $40,000. In a separate deal, Snuffy sells Oscar a $600 set of spare parts that Snuffy bought years after the motorcycle; Oscar pays for and keeps the parts. Snuffy signs only a receipt for the parts, which never mentions the motorcycle. Snuffy then sells the motorcycle to someone else. Can Oscar enforce the motorcycle deal?
o: Yes, because the signed receipt and Oscar's notes can be read together.
Yes, because Oscar paid for and accepted the parts, which counts as part performance of the overall deal.
No, because the parts aren't part of the motorcycle and no signed record covers the motorcycle.
No, because the statute of frauds does not apply between two non-merchants.
Yes, if Oscar shows reasonable reliance under promissory estoppel.
oe: Papers are read together only if they are connected. The receipt never refers to a motorcycle sale.
Part performance reaches only the goods paid for and accepted. The parts and the motorcycle aren't one commercial unit (compare the boat and software in Casazza).
Correct. As in Casazza, accepting a separately bought add-on isn't accepting the main item, and the only signed paper doesn't show a sale of the motorcycle.
It applies to any sale of goods for $500 or more, merchants or not. Oscar loses for a different reason.
Casazza held promissory estoppel couldn't get around § 2-201 on reliance like this.
topic: 3 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Part performance: separate unit

q: On March 1, Kermit sends a supplier a justified written demand for adequate assurance. The supplier ignores it. By April 10, Kermit has heard nothing. What may Kermit do?
o: Cancel only after sending a second demand.
Nothing, because Kermit must sue to compel a response.
Treat the contract as repudiated and pursue its remedies.
Treat the contract as repudiated only if the supplier also misses a delivery.
None of the above.
oe: One justified demand is enough.
Silence has a statutory consequence.
Failing to respond is itself a repudiation.
C is correct.
topic: 15 · Insecurity & repudiation — No response within 30 days

q: A contract reads "F.O.B. Buyer's store, Wilmington." The goods are destroyed in a fire at the carrier's terminal in Baltimore, halfway through the trip. Who bears the loss?
o: The seller, because this is a destination contract.
The buyer, because F.O.B. terms create shipment contracts.
The carrier, because the goods were in its terminal.
The buyer, because the seller had delivered the goods to a carrier.
None of the above.
oe: Only F.O.B. the place of shipment does.
The question is which party bears risk.
That's the shipment-contract rule.
A is correct.
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — F.O.B. buyer's city

q: Fozzie Fabrication sends Gonzo Greenhouses a written proposal to sell two irrigation pumps; its attached terms require any warranty suit within 9 months of delivery. Gonzo accepts with its own purchase order, whose back-page boilerplate "reserves all rights and remedies available at law" and says "acceptance is expressly limited to the terms of this order." The pumps sit in storage for a year and prove defective. Gonzo sues 14 months after delivery. What is the most likely result?
o: The suit is timely, because the conflicting terms knock out and the Code's four-year period applies.
The suit is barred, because Gonzo's purchase order was a counteroffer that Fozzie accepted by shipping.
The suit is timely, because the last form sent always controls.
The suit is barred, because Fozzie's offer controls and its 9-month limit governs.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. As in Daitom, the PO was an acceptance, the shortened period and the reservation of remedies are different terms that drop out (cmt. 6), and § 2-725's four years applies.

"Expressly limited to the terms of this order" is not "expressly conditional" on assent (Daitom), so the PO was an acceptance. And even as a counteroffer, Gonzo's terms would not include the 9-month limit.
§ 2-207 abolished the "last shot" rule.
The offeror's terms don't automatically win. Gonzo's reservation of its legal remedies conflicts with the 9-month limit.
A is correct.
topic: 2 · Formation — Knockout: limitations period

q: A contract calls for a seller to ship machine parts by rail to the buyer's dock. A flood washes out the only rail line to the buyer's town, without fault of either party. Trucks can deliver the parts at a slightly higher cost. What must happen?
o: The seller is excused until the rail line reopens.
The contract is avoided.
The buyer may cancel, because the agreed manner of delivery by rail failed without the buyer's fault.
The seller must tender, and the buyer accept, a reasonable substitute.
None of the above.
oe: A commercially reasonable substitute must be used.
A substitute is available.
The buyer must accept a commercially reasonable substitute.
D is correct.
topic: 16 · Excuse from performance — Substituted performance

q: Grover's order form states: "This acceptance is expressly conditional on Seller's assent to the additional terms below; Buyer will not proceed without that assent." The seller never assents but ships the goods, and Grover pays. They later dispute one of Grover's additional terms. What are the terms of the contract?
o: The terms on which the writings agree, plus the Code's gap fillers.
Whatever terms a court finds most reasonable.
Grover's terms, because the seller shipped after reading them.
The seller's terms, because Grover's form was a counteroffer the seller rejected.
There is no contract, because the seller never assented to Grover's terms.
oe: Correct. Grover's form was expressly conditional, so the writings formed no contract. The parties' conduct did, and § 2-207(3) supplies the terms: those the writings agree on plus supplementary terms under the Code.
The court doesn't pick terms freely. § 2-207(3) tells it which terms count.
Shipping is conduct recognizing a contract, not assent to the extra terms. § 2-207(3) supplies the terms.
The seller's terms don't win by default either.
Shipment and payment are conduct that recognizes a contract (§ 2-207(3)).
topic: 2 · Formation — Expressly conditional; § 2-207(3)

q: A seller of custom brackets sells on 15-day credit terms. It learns that the buyer's credit rating has dropped and that the buyer is paying other vendors slowly, though the buyer isn't insolvent. Which response best protects the seller without risking its own breach?
o: Stop all deliveries without explanation until the buyer's rating improves.
Cancel the contract and resell the brackets.
Send a written demand for adequate assurance, offering several acceptable forms, and suspend if commercially reasonable until it arrives.
Announce that all future deliveries will be cash on delivery.
None of the above.
oe: Suspending without a written demand risks breach.
No repudiation has occurred yet.
Correct. Problem 6-3: use § 2-609, list the grounds, offer options, and set a deadline within 30 days.
Only an insolvent buyer can be put on cash terms (§ 2-702(1)); changing credit terms unilaterally risks repudiation.
C is correct.
topic: 15 · Insecurity & repudiation — Responding to a shaky buyer

q: After agreeing orally to buy a private collector's antique carousel horses for $75,000, Big Bird types up the terms and emails them to the collector, who never replies or signs anything. Relying on the deal, Big Bird pays a $2,000 nonrefundable deposit to a moving company and rents climate-controlled storage. The collector backs out. Can Big Bird enforce the deal?
o: Yes, because the collector's silence after the email binds the collector.
Yes, because Big Bird's typed summary is a sufficient record.
No, because the collector signed nothing and no exception or estoppel theory applies.
No, but only because the deal was over $5,000.
Yes, because Big Bird's reliance on the deal would make the collector's refusal to perform a fraud on Big Bird.
oe: Silence binds only under the merchant's-confirmation exception, which requires both parties to be merchants.
It isn't signed by the party being charged (the collector).
Correct. This tracks Casazza: unsigned typed terms, preparatory reliance, and no exception.
The threshold is $500.
Casazza rejected that argument on similar reliance (a survey and a boat slip).
topic: 3 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Unsigned typed terms; reliance

q: A contract to sell 500 bales of cotton is "C.I.F. Port of Savannah." The seller loads the cotton on a ship, buys insurance, and sends the buyer the documents. The ship sinks before reaching Savannah. Which statement is correct?
o: The buyer bears the loss but may refuse to pay against the documents until it has inspected the cotton.
The buyer bears the loss and must pay against the documents, and it can claim on the insurance.
The seller bears the loss, because the goods never reached the named port.
The seller bears the loss, because it agreed to pay freight and insurance to Savannah.
None of the above.
oe: C.I.F. requires payment against documents, without inspection first.
Correct. A C.I.F. contract is a shipment contract (§ 2-320); risk passed at shipment, and the insurance the seller bought protects the buyer.
The named port is the destination of the freight, not the point where risk passes.
C.I.F. is still a shipment contract.
B is correct.
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — C.I.F.

q: Under a contract for 12 monthly deliveries of cardboard boxes, the third delivery is 2% short, and the seller promptly offers to make up the shortfall within the week. The buyer rejects the whole third delivery. Was the rejection proper?
o: Yes, because a buyer may reject any installment that is late or short.
Yes, because the perfect tender rule lets the buyer reject for any shortfall.
No, because a buyer may never reject an installment.
Yes, because the shortfall breached the whole contract.
None of the above.
oe: Only if the defect substantially impairs that installment and can't be cured.
Not in an installment contract.
It may, when the § 2-612(2) test is met.
A 2% curable shortfall doesn't substantially impair the whole.

Correct. The rejection was improper: in an installment contract, a buyer may reject an installment only if the nonconformity substantially impairs its value and can't be cured (§ 2-612(2)), and a 2% shortfall the seller offers to fix within the week fails that test. No choice says that.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — Installment contract

q: Animal orders a salad at a restaurant. The menu calls the olives "pitted," but Animal cracks a tooth on an olive pit. Animal sues for breach of the implied warranty of merchantability. Which argument best supports the restaurant?
o: The restaurant was not negligent in preparing the salad.
Animal can sue only the olive grower, not the restaurant.
Food served in a restaurant is a service, not a sale of goods.
Pits are natural to olives, so under the foreign-natural test the salad was fit for its ordinary purpose.
None of the above.
oe: Merchantability is strict liability; negligence doesn't matter.
The restaurant, a merchant seller of food, gives the warranty.
§ 2-314(1): serving food or drink for value is a sale.
Correct. That's the approach usually tied to Webster v. Blue Ship Tea Room (fish bones in chowder). Under the reasonable-expectation test, "pitted" would help Animal.
D is correct.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Food: foreign-natural test

q: Bert agrees to buy a $2,000 drum set and pays a $900 deposit. The contract has no liquidated-damages clause. Bert then repudiates, and the seller resells at no loss and has no other damages. How much of the deposit must the seller return?
o: Nothing, because Bert breached.
$900, because the seller suffered no loss.
oe: A breaching buyer still gets restitution of the excess.
The seller may keep the smaller of 20% of the price or $500.
Correct. § 2-718(2)(b): the seller may keep the smaller of 20% of the price ($400) or $500, so it keeps $400 and returns $500.
That would mean keeping only $200.
That's what the seller keeps, not what it returns.
topic: 11 · Remedies & remedy limitations — Deposit restitution

q: A written contract describes a boat engine as a "2025 model, 250 horsepower," and later states in bold type: "SELLER MAKES NO WARRANTIES, EXPRESS OR IMPLIED." The engine is a 2019 model with 180 horsepower. Is the description an enforceable express warranty?
o: No, because "no warranties, express or implied" disclaims every warranty.
No, because the bold disclaimer is conspicuous.
Yes, because the disclaimer can't be reconciled with the description.
Yes, but only if the buyer relied on the description.
None of the above.
oe: Not an express warranty in the same writing.
Conspicuousness can't save a disclaimer that contradicts an express warranty.
A warranty in the written contract needs no proof of reliance.
C is correct.
topic: 10 · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Express warranty vs. disclaimer

q: A packaging supplier's resin costs double after a fire at its main resin source. The supplier shows Elmo the numbers and asks for a 15% price increase for the rest of the year, making clear it will keep delivering at the old price if Elmo says no. Elmo signs a modification agreeing to the increase, then refuses to pay it. Is the modification enforceable?
o: No, because the supplier gave no new consideration.
No, because higher costs don't excuse performance under § 2-615.
Yes, but only if a court finds 15% to be a reasonable amount.
Yes, because it was sought in good faith.
None of the above.
oe: None is needed (§ 2-209(1)).
Excuse and modification are different. A market shift can justify asking for a modification even if it wouldn't excuse performance (cmt. 2).
The test is good faith, not the reasonableness of the new price.
Correct. Both parts of good faith are met: an objective commercial reason and honesty in fact. Compare Roth Steel, where the threat was the problem.
D is correct.
topic: 4 · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Modification sought in good faith

q: A contract's only integration clause reads: "This agreement supersedes all prior agreements, written or oral." The buyer claims that at the signing table, the seller orally promised free installation. Why might the clause fail to keep that evidence out?
o: Because the clause speaks only of prior agreements and never says the writing is complete and exclusive.
Because an oral promise at signing is treated as a later modification.
Because merger clauses are unenforceable in consumer contracts.
Because the clause wasn't separately signed.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Problem 5-11: "supersedes all prior agreements" misses contemporaneous terms; pair it with "complete and exclusive statement."
A promise at signing is contemporaneous, not later.
They can be enforced, though they're not conclusive.
No separate signature is needed.
A is correct.
topic: 12 · Parol evidence rule — "Supersedes prior agreements"

q: Under an open-price contract, a fertilizer supplier charges every customer its published list price, which tracks the market. Nothing suggests an improper motive. A buyer argues the price is too high. What is the likely result?
o: The buyer wins, because a seller-set price must equal the seller's cost plus a reasonable profit.
The buyer wins, because a seller-set price must be renegotiated each time.
The buyer wins, because open-price terms are unenforceable.
The supplier wins, because a price set by one party is never reviewable.
None of the above.
oe: No cost-plus rule exists.
§ 2-305(2) lets one party set the price.
§ 2-305 makes them enforceable.
It must be set in good faith.
Correct. The supplier wins: in the normal case, a posted price or a price in effect in the market satisfies the good-faith requirement (§ 2-305 cmt. 3). No choice says that.
topic: 7 · Quantity & price — Posted price safe harbor

q: Big Bird leaves an oil painting at a frame shop to be reframed. The shop sells frames and framing services but never sells artwork. The shop's owner sells the painting to a customer who pays fair value in good faith. Big Bird sues the customer. Who wins?
o: Big Bird, because the shop doesn't sell paintings.
Big Bird, but only if the shop's owner is convicted of theft.
The customer, because the customer paid fair value in good faith.
The customer, because Big Bird entrusted the painting to a merchant.
The customer, because the frame shop had voidable title.
oe: Correct. § 2-403(2) applies only to a merchant who deals in goods of that kind.
A conviction isn't required.
Good faith doesn't help unless the seller had voidable title or the entrustment power.
Entrustment requires a merchant who deals in goods of that kind, meaning paintings.
A bailee holding goods for repair has no title at all.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Entrustment: shop that doesn't sell

q: Statler's supplier delegates its duty to deliver 500 cases of popcorn to a new, unknown company. Under § 2-210, what may Statler do?
o: Refuse to deal with the new company without giving any reason.
Treat the delegation as a repudiation and cancel immediately.
Nothing, because delegation of standard goods is always allowed.
Demand assurances from the new company.
None of the above.
oe: Statler must accept a valid delegation, but it may demand assurances.
Delegation of standard goods isn't a repudiation.
Allowed, but the statute gives Statler a way to protect itself.
D is correct.
topic: 13 · Assignment & delegation — Delegation as grounds for insecurity

q: The Count, an art dealer, sells Zoe a lamp for $90,000 under a signed bill of sale warranting that it is "an authentic Tiffany Studios lamp." Before closing, Zoe's own appraiser tells Zoe the lamp may be a reproduction. Zoe closes anyway. The lamp is a fake. Can Zoe recover for breach of express warranty?
o: No, because Zoe did not believe the warranty at closing.
Yes, because the doubts came from Zoe's appraiser, not the seller, so Zoe could still buy the promise.
Yes, but only if Zoe expressly reserved rights at closing.
No, because a dealer's statement about authenticity is only an opinion.
No, because Zoe's knowledge before closing kept the warranty from being part of the basis of the bargain.
oe: Belief isn't the test. The question is whether Zoe bought the seller's promise (Rogath).
Correct. Under Rogath, a buyer who hears doubts from someone other than the seller may still rely on the warranty as insurance against that very risk.
A reservation matters when the seller disclosed the problem. Here the seller didn't.
A written warranty of authenticity is an affirmation of fact.
Knowledge from a third party doesn't defeat the warranty.
topic: 5 · Express warranties — Basis of the bargain: third-party doubts
